description_authors_words: we introduce SWE-bench, an evaluation framework consisting of $2,294$ software engineering problems drawn from real GitHub issues and corresponding pull requests across $12$ popular Python repositories.
description_summary: Given a GitHub issue and a repo snapshot, a model must generate a code patch that makes the project's held-out fail-to-pass tests pass, across 12 real Python codebases.
task_format_metric: patch correctness verified by test-suite execution (fail-to-pass / pass-to-pass tests)
example_length: 1.7 other:files (files edited per reference solution (average)) | 32.8 other:lines (lines added/removed per reference solution (average)) | 438000 other:lines (codebase size in lines of code that must fit in context (average))
what_instead_if_absent: The paper never uses 'long-term' or 'long-horizon' anywhere in the text; it frames its core difficulty via 'extremely long contexts' — the size of the codebase a model must process (438K lines on average) — a long-CONTEXT-WINDOW framing rather than a long-horizon EXECUTION framing, consistent with its single-shot (non-agentic) evaluation protocol.
evidence_span: Resolving issues in SWE-bench frequently requires understanding and coordinating changes across multiple functions, classes, and even files simultaneously, calling for models to interact with execution environments, process extremely long contexts and perform complex reasoning that goes far beyond traditional code generation tasks.
scope_flag: In its original form (as evaluated in this paper), SWE-bench is a single-shot retrieval+generation task (given a codebase and issue description, produce a patch) rather than a multi-turn agentic execution benchmark; the paper explicitly frames the core difficulty as processing 'extremely long contexts' from a large codebase and explicitly defers agent-based/multi-turn approaches to future work ('we do not intend to constrain future methodologies to the same type of approach... e.g., agent-based approaches'). Its very common later use as a long-horizon coding-agent benchmark (via SWE-agent-style harnesses) is not part of this paper's own contribution, making the long-horizon-execution charter fit borderline for the paper as published (kept in-corpus; flagged for the aggregate to weigh).

description_authors_words: We introduce WebArena, a realistic and reproducible web environment designed to facilitate the development of autonomous agents capable of executing tasks.
description_summary: Autonomous agents must complete multi-step tasks (shopping, forum posts, code hosting, etc.) inside a realistic self-hosted web environment, scored by functional/exact-match success checks.
external_memory_evidence: These intermediate states are often the underlying databases of the websites, the status, and the content of a web page at each step of the execution.
task_format_metric: exact/fuzzy match + program-based functional correctness on web task completion
what_instead_if_absent: the paper elsewhere 'formally defines' the general agent-control task (natural language instruction -> sequence of actions), but never pins down what specifically makes tasks 'long-horizon' with a turn/step criterion; 'long-horizon' is asserted only as a descriptive property of the released 812 tasks
evidence_span: The tasks in our benchmark are diverse, long-horizon, and designed to emulate tasks that humans routinely perform on the internet.

description_authors_words: We introduce Mind2Web, the first dataset for developing and evaluating generalist agents for the web that can follow language instructions to complete complex tasks on any website.
description_summary: Web-agent benchmark of 2,000+ open-ended tasks on 137 real (not simulated) websites, scored against crowdsourced action sequences for following language instructions.
task_format_metric: Element Accuracy + Operation F1 + Step Success Rate + task-level Success Rate
example_length: 14 actions (actions required for one illustrated example task (Figure 1(b))) | 1000 other:DOM elements (average number of elements per webpage (over 1,000, later cleaned to 580))
what_instead_if_absent: the paper contrasts its own 'high-level goal' setting against prior work's step-by-step directives, and notes existing research 'primarily concentrates on short-term tool invocation, neglecting long-term planning' -- but the latter is a critique of prior work in the discussion, not an explicit definition of what makes Mind2Web's own tasks long-term/long-horizon
evidence_span: However, existing research primarily concentrates on short-term tool invocation, neglecting long-term planning.

description_authors_words: we develop WebShop -- a simulated e-commerce website environment with $1.18$ million real-world products and $12,087$ crowd-sourced text instructions
description_summary: Tests whether a web agent can find, customize, and purchase a specific product on a simulated e-commerce site with 1.18M real products, given a natural-language shopping instruction.
task_format_metric: Task Score (avg. reward) + Success Rate over shopping trajectories
example_length: 11.3–114 other:states (states visited per trajectory (human-expert average)) | 1.9–16 other:items (unique items checked per trajectory (human-expert average)) | 1.4–16 other:searches (searches per trajectory (human-expert average))
length_unit_families: agent steps / actions; stored memory items
long_horizon_definition: [explicit-stated] long-term memory for comparing items or backtracking, illustrated by a worked example: a human explores several products, then returns to the first-explored product — a backtracking behavior the IL+RL baseline model lacks
evidence_span: 4) long-term memory for comparing items or backtracking (Figure 1)... In the second example, the human explores several products first, and decides to return to the first explored product, demonstrating long-term memory that is lacking in the IL+RL model.

description_authors_words: We introduce a new 'deep memory retrieval' (DMR) task based on the MSC dataset designed to test the consistency of a conversational agent.
description_summary: Introduces MemGPT, an OS-inspired LLM memory-management system; its own eval, Deep Memory Retrieval, tests whether an agent can answer questions requiring recall from much earlier chat sessions.
external_memory_evidence: LLM agents can read and write to external data sources, modify their own context, and choose when to return responses to the user.
task_format_metric: Deep Memory Retrieval accuracy (LLM-judged) + conversation-opener similarity (SIM-1/3, SIM-H); document-analysis QA/KV-retrieval accuracy
long_horizon_definition: [operational-threshold] Conversational agents like virtual companions and personalized assistants aim to engage users in natural, long-term interactions, potentially spanning weeks, months, or even years. This creates challenges for models with fixed-length contexts, which can only reference a limited history of the conversation.
evidence_span: Conversational agents like virtual companions and personalized assistants aim to engage users in natural, long-term interactions, potentially spanning weeks, months, or even years.
scope_flag: MemGPT's primary contribution is a memory-management METHOD/architecture (OS-inspired virtual context management); its evaluation augments the existing Multi-Session Chat dataset with two new tasks (DMR, conversation opener) rather than shipping a wholly new named benchmark artifact.

description_authors_words: We introduced ALFWorld, the first interactive text environment with aligned embodied worlds.
description_summary: Text-based household task simulator aligned one-to-one with the ALFRED embodied benchmark, testing whether abstract TextWorld policies transfer to grounded multi-step action execution.
task_format_metric: task success rate + goal-condition success rate (TextWorld and embodied transfer)
example_length: 50 steps (maximum steps per episode)
what_instead_if_absent: the paper never uses 'long-term' or 'long-horizon' anywhere (confirmed by full-text search); it frames task difficulty via ALFRED's compositional, multi-step household tasks and an 'observation queue length k' ablation parameter for how many past observations the agent can see, without ever labeling this a 'long-horizon' property.
evidence_span: In the first column, we show the effect of using different observation queue lengths k as described in Section 3.1, in which size 0 refers to not providing any observation information to the agent.

description_authors_words: We introduce GAIA, a benchmark for General AI Assistants that, if solved, would represent a milestone in AI research.
description_summary: 466 real-world questions needing reasoning, web browsing, multimodal handling, and tool use, each with one exact-match answer; easy for humans, hard for AI assistants.
task_format_metric: Exact-match accuracy against a unique factual answer
example_length: 5 steps (annotator-counted steps to solve a Level 1 question (no tools, or at most one tool)) | 5–10 steps (annotator-counted steps to solve a Level 2 question, combining different tools)
what_instead_if_absent: the paper never uses 'long-horizon' or 'long-term' (not found in the targeted read); it defines task difficulty entirely via annotator-counted 'number of steps' and 'number of tools' needed to solve a question
evidence_span: The questions can be sorted into three levels of increasing difficulty depending on the number of steps required to solve the questions, and the number of different tools needed to answer the question.

description_authors_words: we introduce OSWorld , the first-of-its-kind scalable, real computer environment for multimodal agents, supporting task setup, execution-based evaluation, and interactive learning across various operating systems such as Ubuntu, Windows, and macOS.
description_summary: Real Ubuntu/Windows/macOS desktop environment where multimodal agents complete open-ended GUI tasks across real applications, graded by execution-based checkers on final system state.
external_memory_evidence: The configuration file specifies the snapshot of the virtual machine to be used (which stores the complete state of a computer at a certain moment and can be restored to this state at any time) and also indicates the information needed for setup (such as downloading files and opening some software, making some additional settings, etc.).
task_format_metric: task success rate (execution-based checkers)
example_length: 15–15 steps (maximum interaction steps allowed per task (experimental cap, not a reported mean))
what_instead_if_absent: the paper repeatedly names 'long-horizon decision-making' and 'long-term user-assistant interactions' as challenges posed by real computer environments (rich multi-app observations, high-res screenshots, accessibility trees) but never pins down a turn/step/time threshold or contrastive baseline that defines what counts as long-horizon.
evidence_span: These raw observations allow rich interactions between multiple applications but induce challenges in long-horizon decision-making from high-resolution images (e.g., 4k screenshots) and structured long text (e.g., accessibility trees).

description_authors_words: We propose $\tau$-bench, a benchmark emulating dynamic conversations between a user (simulated by language models) and a language agent provided with domain-specific API tools and policy guidelines.
description_summary: Tests whether an agent can hold a policy-constrained tool-use conversation with a simulated user, scoring success by matching the final database state to an annotated goal and reliability via pass^k over repeated trials.
external_memory_evidence: We employ an efficient and faithful evaluation process that compares the database state at the end of a conversation with the annotated goal state.
task_format_metric: task success rate (pass^k over multiple trials) via database-state matching against annotated goal state
example_length: 30–30 actions (agent actions (tool calls or user responses) allowed per task)
what_instead_if_absent: The paper asserts that agents must 'interact seamlessly with both humans and programmatic APIs over long horizons' as a desideratum, and later lists 'long-horizon information tracking and memory' as a needed future improvement, but never states what conversation length, turn count, or duration counts as 'long horizon' for τ-bench itself.
evidence_span: Agents must (1) interact seamlessly with both humans and programmatic APIs over long horizons to incrementally gather information and resolve intents

description_authors_words: We show that relation extraction can be reduced to answering simple reading comprehension questions, by associating one or more natural-language questions with each relation slot.
description_summary: Wikipedia relation slot-filling recast as reading-comprehension QA over a sentence, with a zero-shot split testing extraction of unseen relation types; later reused by knowledge-editing work as a generalization/locality probe.
venue: Conference on Computational Natural Language Learning
task_format_metric: span-extraction F1 (reading comprehension over relation slot-filling questions)
what_instead_if_absent: this is the original 2017 zero-shot relation-extraction paper, predating knowledge-editing and LLM-agent framing entirely; it never discusses memory, editing, or long-horizon/long-term constructs at all. The 'zsRE' name is only later repurposed by knowledge-editing papers (ROME, MEND, etc.) as a standard editing testbed -- that repurposing is external to this paper.
evidence_span: We use distant supervision for a relatively large number of relations (120) from Wikidata, which are easily gathered in practice via the WikiReading dataset.

description_authors_words: we collect LoCoMo, a dataset of very long-term conversations, each encompassing 300 turns and 9K tokens on avg., over up to 35 sessions.
description_summary: Tests recall, temporal and multi-hop QA, event summarization, and multimodal dialogue generation over synthetic persona-grounded conversations spanning up to 35 chat sessions.
external_memory_evidence: The long-term memory is a database of observations about each speaker, that are essentially assertive statements about the speaker’s persona and life.
venue: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
task_format_metric: QA accuracy (single-hop/multi-hop/temporal/commonsense/adversarial) + event summarization + LLM-judge for multimodal dialogue generation
example_length: 300 turns (turns per conversation (average)) | 9000 tokens (tokens per conversation (average, '9K tokens')) | 35–35 sessions (sessions per conversation (up to))
length_unit_families: conversational turns; sessions / episodes; tokens / text length
long_horizon_definition: [contrastive] Prior long-term open-domain dialogue evaluation limited itself to contexts of ~1K tokens over at most five chat sessions; this paper instead targets 'very long-term' dialogues that go far beyond that scale.
evidence_span: studies in long-term open-domain dialogues have concentrated on assessing model responses within limited contexts e.g., ∼1K tokens over five chat sessions

description_authors_words: We present a new AI task - Embodied Question Answering (EmbodiedQA) - where an agent is spawned at a random location in a 3D environment and asked a question...
description_summary: An agent spawned in a 3D house must navigate to gather egocentric visual evidence, then answer a natural-language question about what it saw.
venue: 2018 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW)
task_format_metric: navigation success + answer accuracy on templated questions
long_horizon_definition: [contrastive] the paper illustrates what it means by 'long-term memory' via contrasting question types: 'How many bedrooms in the house?' requires significant navigation (potentially exploring the entire environment) and long-term memory (keeping track of the count), while a question like 'What color is the chair in the living room?' requires only finding a single room
evidence_span: a question like 'How many bedrooms in the house?' requires significant navigation (potentially exploring the entire environment) and long-term memory (keeping track of the count), while a question like 'What color is the chair in the living room?' requires finding a single room

description_authors_words: We introduce MemoryBank, a novel mechanism designed to provide LLMs with the ability to retain long-term memory and draw user portraits.
description_summary: Evaluates a companion chatbot's ability to recall and update user-specific facts over a 10-day multi-session dialogue, with human-like forgetting of older memories.
external_memory_evidence: These vector representations are then indexed using FAISS ( Johnson et al., 2019 ) for efficient retrieval.
task_format_metric: memory-recall QA accuracy (probing questions) + personality/empathy assessment
example_length: 10 days (length of the simulated long-term dialogue history (memory storage) used for evaluation)
long_horizon_definition: [explicit-stated] The Ebbinghaus forgetting curve is expressed using an exponential decay model: R = e^(-t/S), where R is the memory retention... t is the time elapsed since learning the information... S is the memory strength... When a memory item is recalled during conversations, it will persist longer in memory. We increase S by 1 and reset t to 0, hence forget it with a lower probability.
evidence_span: The Ebbinghaus forgetting curve is expressed using an exponential decay model: R=e^{-t/S}, where R is the memory retention, or what fraction of the information can be retained.

description_authors_words: We introduce LongMemEval, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate five core long-term memory abilities of chat assistants: information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention.
description_summary: Tests five long-term memory abilities of chat assistants (extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, abstention) via QA over synthetic multi-session chat histories up to 1.5M tokens.
task_format_metric: QA accuracy over 500 curated questions + retrieval recall@k
example_length: 115000 tokens (tokens per chat history, LongMemEval-S setting) | 500 sessions (sessions per chat history, LongMemEval-M setting) | 1500000 tokens (tokens per chat history, LongMemEval-M setting)
long_horizon_definition: [explicit-stated] long-term memory, the ability to memorize, recall, and reason with a long interaction history
evidence_span: To personalize LLM-based assistants, long-term memory, the ability to memorize, recall, and reason with a long interaction history, is indispensable.

description_authors_words: We introduce MineDojo, a new framework built on the popular Minecraft game that features a simulation suite with thousands of diverse open-ended tasks and an internet-scale knowledge base with Minecraft videos, tutorials, wiki pages, and forum discussions.
description_summary: Long-horizon, open-ended task suite in Minecraft (3000+ language-specified goals) testing whether embodied agents can acquire and reuse skills using internet-scale video/wiki knowledge as a reward signal.
task_format_metric: programmatic task success rate (simulator-verified); Creative task success via MineCLIP reward model
example_length: 100000 steps (order-of-magnitude step count for the hardest programmatic task (Playthrough: defeating the Ender Dragon), described as 'hundreds of thousands of steps')
long_horizon_definition: [operational-threshold] the paper labels its hardest task (Playthrough, defeating the Ender Dragon) as 'extremely long horizon (hundreds of thousands of steps)', contrasted with standard programmatic tasks that 'require fewer steps and lower resource dependencies'; it separately describes its broader Creative task suite as containing 'long-horizon, open-ended tasks that cannot be easily evaluated through automated procedures'
evidence_span: It would be extremely long horizon (hundreds of thousands of steps) and difficult for an agent to tackle. We consider this one of the moonshot goals in MineDojo.

description_authors_words: We present BrowseComp, a simple yet challenging benchmark for measuring the ability for agents to browse the web.
description_summary: Web-browsing agents answer 1,266 hard-to-find factual questions requiring persistent multi-step search, graded by exact match against short, easily verified reference answers.
task_format_metric: short-answer accuracy verified against reference answers
example_length: 0–300 other:minutes (human time-to-solve one question, per histogram (axis range, not a stated mean))
what_instead_if_absent: The paper never uses 'long-term' or 'long-horizon' anywhere in the text; it frames its core difficulty entirely through 'persistence' — 'exercising persistence and creativity in finding information' — rather than a temporal-horizon construct.
evidence_span: While BrowseComp sidesteps challenges of a true user query distribution, like generating long answers or resolving ambiguity, it measures the important core capability of exercising persistence and creativity in finding information.

description_authors_words: we introduce three challenging language model editing problems based on question answering, fact-checking, and dialogue generation
description_summary: Tests whether a model edit stays scoped: QA, fact-checking, and dialogue tasks score edit success and drawdown on unrelated inputs after a single knowledge edit.
external_memory_evidence: As a higher-capacity alternative, we propose Semi-Parametric Editing with a Retrieval-Augmented Counterfactual Model (SERAC), which stores edits in an explicit memory and learns to reason over them to modulate the base model’s predictions as needed.
task_format_metric: Edit Success (ES) and Drawdown (DD) across QA, QA-hard, FC, and ConvSent editing problems
example_length: 10–75 other:edits (simultaneous/sequential edits applied per evaluation batch (QA, QA-hard, FC settings; k=5 for ConvSent))
what_instead_if_absent: the paper is entirely about scaling the NUMBER of simultaneous/sequential model edits (k), not duration or session count; it never uses 'long-horizon'/'long-term', instead evaluating editors on batches of k in {1,5,10,25,75} edits and showing SERAC's edit-memory approach gives identical results whether edits are applied in sequence or simultaneously
evidence_span: SERAC applies up to 75 edits with little degradation of edit performance; ENN and MEND approach complete failure for 75 edits.

aliases: LaMP-1; LaMP-2; LaMP-3; LaMP-4; LaMP-5; LaMP-6; LaMP-7
description_authors_words: This paper highlights the importance of personalization in large language models and introduces the LaMP benchmark — a novel benchmark for training and evaluating language models for producing personalized outputs.
description_summary: Personalization benchmark where a model generates or classifies short text (headlines, ratings, tags) conditioned on a user's own retrieved historical profile items, scored per task.
external_memory_evidence: We explore various choices for the retrieval model ℛ \mathcal{R} . In our experiments, we study a strong term matching model, BM25 Robertson et al. (1995) , a state-of-the-art pre-trained dense retrieval model, Contriever Izacard et al. (2022) , a retrieval model that returns most recent profile entries in descending order (i.e., Recency), and a Random document selector from the user profile.
venue: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
task_format_metric: task-specific accuracy/F1 (classification tasks) and ROUGE/METEOR (generation tasks), personalized via retrieval-augmented user profile
example_length: 15 other:profile_items (user profile size (number of past items), smallest task (Personalized Tweet Paraphrasing, user split)) | 287.16 other:profile_items (user profile size (number of past items), largest task (Personalized News Headline Generation, user split)) | 9.78 tokens (output length, News Headline Generation (average))
length_unit_families: stored memory items; tokens / text length
what_instead_if_absent: the paper never uses 'long-horizon' or 'long-term' in its own defining prose (the only occurrence is inside a cited reference's title, 'Modeling the impact of short- and long-term behavior on search personalization'); it instead formally defines a 'user profile' as the user's historical data P_u = {(x_u1,y_u1),...,(x_u,m_u,y_u,m_u)}, without any duration-based criterion
evidence_span: In LaMP, we define user profile as the user's historical data, i.e., the past input and personalized outputs produced by or approved by the user, P_u = {(x_u1,y_u1),(x_u2,y_u2),...,(x_u,m_u,y_u,m_u)}.

description_authors_words: In order to address this gap, we introduce τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench, with a dual-control environment, where (LLM-simulated) users can take actions and call tools in addition to communicating with the agent.
description_summary: Extends tau-bench to a dual-control setting where both agent and simulated user can call tools, testing coordination and state-tracking in shared dynamic environments like telecom support.
external_memory_evidence: The agent have access to a set of tools that interact with a database, and is tasked with resolving the user’s request via Tool-Agent-User (TAU) interactions while adhering to the domain policy. To test real-world scenarios, the user is simulated by another AI agent given a scenario-based instruction and a set of tools that interact with its own database.
task_format_metric: pass^1 task success rate, binned by number of actions/subtasks required
example_length: 7–10 actions (number of actions required to solve a task, at which performance drops to near zero in Default mode)
long_horizon_definition: [operational-threshold] the paper uses number of actions/subtasks required to solve a task as a proxy for difficulty and, in analyzing results, explicitly refers to tasks requiring more actions (performance dropping near zero at 7+ actions in Default mode, with a distinct tail at 10+ actions) as 'longer-horizon tasks'
evidence_span: This hints that maintaining reliability over longer-horizon tasks remains a challenge under both settings and communication with the user is not the only bottleneck.

description_authors_words: we introduce FreshQA, a novel dynamic QA benchmark encompassing a diverse range of question and answer types, including questions that require fast-changing world knowledge as well as questions with false premises that need to be debunked
description_summary: Open-domain QA testing whether models track fast-changing real-world facts and detect false-premise questions, judged under a two-mode (relaxed/strict) human protocol plus an automatic FreshEval judge.
venue: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
task_format_metric: two-mode human evaluation (Relaxed / Strict correctness) + FreshEval automatic judge
what_instead_if_absent: the paper never uses 'long-horizon'/'long-term'; it instead defines four temporal-change categories for its questions -- never-changing, slow-changing (answer typically changes over the course of several years), fast-changing (answer typically changes within a year or less), and false-premise -- as its operational framework for knowledge freshness
evidence_span: never-changing , in which the answer almost never changes; slow-changing , in which the answer typically changes over the course of several years; fast-changing , in which the answer typically changes within a year or less; and false-premise , which includes questions whose premises are factually incorrect and thus have to be rebutted.

description_authors_words: our first contribution in this paper is a diagnostic dataset, TempLAMA (short for TEMPoral LAnguage Model Analysis), of fill-in-the-blank queries for probing time-sensitive knowledge in LMs.
description_summary: Cloze-style fact-probing dataset where the correct fill-in answer to a query changes across years, testing whether a language model's stored knowledge tracks the right time period.
venue: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics
task_format_metric: F1 score (macro-averaged across evaluation years)
what_instead_if_absent: the paper never uses 'long-horizon'/'long-term'; it frames its task as time-scoped cloze QA evaluated across yearly slices (2010-2020), studying model 'forgetting' and generalization to future/past year slices, without invoking horizon/duration vocabulary as a named construct.
evidence_span: The performance drop on both sides shows the forgetting effect.

description_authors_words: we present Terminal-Bench 2.0: a carefully curated hard benchmark composed of 89 tasks in computer terminal environments inspired by problems from real workflows.
description_summary: 89 realistic command-line tasks in isolated terminal environments, each with a human-written solution and test suite, scoring whether an agent completes a full real-world workflow.
task_format_metric: task resolution rate against human-written solutions and comprehensive test suites
example_length: 1–168 hours (expert time-estimate to complete a task (dominant bucket: 1h-24h covers ~47% of tasks; <1h covers ~49%))
long_horizon_definition: [operational-threshold] The paper ties 'long-horizon' directly to measured task-completion cost: expert/junior engineer time estimates ranging up to 240 hours (10 days) for the hardest task, and agent trials taking up to two hours with hundreds of API calls and ~100 million tokens on a single task.
evidence_span: One task, fix-ocaml-gc, requires the agent to fix the OCaml garbage collector after an attempted but failed optimization and takes almost 1 day (24 hours) for an expert and ten days (240 hours) for a junior engineer to complete, highlighting the ability of the Terminal-Bench framework to express complex, long-horizon tasks.

description_authors_words: We present the first comprehensive and controlled investigation into the behavior of LLMs when encountering knowledge conflicts.
description_summary: Tests whether an LLM answers questions using its own parametric knowledge or switches to conflicting counter-memory evidence injected into the prompt context, over PopQA and StrategyQA.
task_format_metric: memorization ratio (parametric-memory vs. counter-memory answer selection) across PopQA and StrategyQA
what_instead_if_absent: the paper never uses 'long-horizon' or 'long-term'; it frames its problem entirely as single-turn closed-book vs. counter-memory QA (parametric memory vs. external conflicting evidence), with no session/duration dimension
evidence_span: Step 1 in Figure 1 illustrates how we elicit parametric memory: in a closed-book QA fashion, LLMs recall their parametric memory to answer questions without any external evidence.

description_authors_words: we introduce MLE-bench, a benchmark for measuring how well AI agents perform at machine learning engineering
description_summary: Tests whether an AI agent can perform real machine learning engineering by completing 75 Kaggle competitions end-to-end, scored against human Kaggle leaderboard medal thresholds.
external_memory_evidence: Each agent has full write access to a 4095 GiB SSD which it uses to produce its final submission and create any intermediate files.
task_format_metric: Kaggle medal rate (bronze/silver/gold) vs. human leaderboards
example_length: 24–100 hours (agent wall-clock time budget per competition attempt (main experiment; extended to 100 hours in an ablation))
what_instead_if_absent: the paper never uses 'long-horizon'/'long-term'; it frames difficulty entirely via wall-clock time budget (24-hour default, up to 100-hour ablation) and a human-solve-time-estimated 'complexity level' (Low <2hrs, Medium 2-10hrs, High >10hrs), without ever invoking horizon/duration terminology as a named construct.
evidence_span: Complexity is defined as: Low if we estimate that an experienced ML engineer can produce a sensible solution in under 2 hours excluding the time taken to train any models, Medium if it takes between 2 and 10 hours, and High if it takes more than 10 hours.

description_authors_words: The dataset consists of human-human crowdworker chats over 5 sessions, with each session consisting of up to 14 utterances, where the conversationalists reengage after a number of hours or days and continue chatting.
description_summary: Human-human crowdworker dialogues spanning 5 chat sessions with time gaps between sessions, testing whether models can recall and build on earlier-session content when conversation resumes.

(2021) ; and (ii) a proposed read-write memory-based model that summarizes and stores conversation on the fly.

example_length: 12500–20000 other:screenshots (screenshots collected per user, spanning one month of computer usage (range 5,000-20,000)) | 26000 tokens (average conversation length in the LOCOMO comparison dataset (10 conversations, 600 dialogues each))
long_horizon_definition: [contrastive] cognitive science's short-term (working) memory vs. long-term memory distinction is adopted, with short-term mapped to the LLM's input context window and long-term treated (critically, by the paper's own account) as 'a catch-all category for any information outside the context'; MIRIX's own six-component architecture (Core/Episodic/Semantic/Procedural/Resource/Knowledge-Vault) is proposed specifically to replace this catch-all with finer-grained structure
evidence_span: Cognitive science broadly categorizes memory into short-term (working) memory and long-term memory. In the context of LLMs, short-term memory is often mapped to the input context window, while long-term memory becomes a catch-all category for any information outside the context.

description_authors_words: we introduce TemporalWiki, a lifelong benchmark for ever-evolving LMs that utilizes the difference between consecutive snapshots of English Wikipedia and English Wikidata for training and evaluation, respectively.
description_summary: Tests whether continually-updated language models retain old facts and learn new ones, using diffs between consecutive Wikipedia/Wikidata snapshots as train/eval data across time.
venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
task_format_metric: perplexity on proper-noun tokens (Changed vs. Unchanged factual instances) across successive snapshots
example_length: 512 tokens (fixed input length per sampled evaluation instance (for perplexity measurement))
what_instead_if_absent: The paper never uses 'long-term' or 'long-horizon' anywhere in the text; it frames its temporal-persistence dimension entirely through 'lifelong'/'ever-evolving' language models and 'temporal misalignment' (misalignment in time between train and test data), evaluated via periodic Wikipedia/Wikidata snapshot diffs.
evidence_span: In this paper, we introduce TemporalWiki, a lifelong benchmark for training and evaluating ever-evolving LMs in a periodic and automated manner... which we name as TWiki-Diffsets.

description_authors_words: We introduce PrefEval, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs' ability to infer, memorize and adhere to user preferences in a long-context conversational setting.
description_summary: Chat assistants must infer user preferences stated earlier in a long conversation and later apply them, tested via generation and multiple-choice tasks over contexts up to 100k tokens.
task_format_metric: LLM-judge preference-following accuracy (generation task) + MCQ classification accuracy
example_length: 10–300 turns (conversation turns between preference disclosure and final query) | 3000–103000 tokens (token length of the intervening context between preference disclosure and final query)
what_instead_if_absent: the paper uses 'long-context' and 'multi-session' repeatedly to describe its setting but never defines a threshold or contrast for what counts as long; it is used as an unexamined given
evidence_span: This presents a challenge for the LLM to accurately infer, retain, and retrieve user preferences while navigating unrelated dialogues, assessing the LLM's ability to handle long-context preference following.

description_authors_words: we construct a new large-scale dataset, StreamingQA, with human written and generated questions asked on a given date, to be answered from 14 years of time-stamped news articles
description_summary: QA over 14 years of dated news, evaluated quarterly as models see new articles, to test whether parametric or semi-parametric updating keeps answers current without catastrophic forgetting.
task_format_metric: F1 / exact-match QA accuracy over quarterly time-sliced news streams
what_instead_if_absent: the paper's operative framing is a 'streaming task' with quarterly temporal splits used to measure 'adaptation and forgetting', with no occurrence of 'long-horizon'/'long-term' terminology anywhere in the sections searched
evidence_span: We consider a streaming task: we split questions into four quarterly sets over 2020 based on their question dates, where questions in each quarter are to be answered from articles published up to and including that quarter.

description_authors_words: we introduce the Comprehensive RAG Benchmark (CRAG) , a factual question answering benchmark of 4,409 question-answer pairs and mock APIs to simulate web and Knowledge Graph (KG) search.
description_summary: 4,409 factual QA pairs with mock web/knowledge-graph search APIs spanning five domains, testing RAG systems on questions of varying entity popularity and temporal volatility, judged for truthfulness.
external_memory_evidence: we introduce the Comprehensive RAG Benchmark (CRAG) , a factual question answering benchmark of 4,409 question-answer pairs and mock APIs to simulate web and Knowledge Graph (KG) search.
task_format_metric: truthfulness score (accurate/acceptable/missing/incorrect, human + auto-evaluator) on factual QA
what_instead_if_absent: the paper never uses 'long-horizon' or 'long-term' anywhere in the cached text; instead it defines a 'dynamism' taxonomy (real-time, fast-changing, slow-changing, static) for how quickly a fact's ground truth can change over calendar time
evidence_span: CRAG is designed to encapsulate a diverse array of questions across five domains and eight question categories, reflecting varied entity popularity from popular to long-tail, and temporal dynamisms ranging from years to seconds.
scope_flag: CRAG is a single-turn factual QA / RAG-freshness benchmark: each example is one independent question-answer pair tested against time-varying facts (real-time/fast-changing/slow-changing/static dynamism categories); there is no session, trajectory, or persistent interaction history for an agent to carry state across. It fits the charter's 'temporal reasoning over an evolving history' clause only in the weak sense that facts themselves change over calendar time, not that the system must track or update memory across turns.

description_authors_words: we introduce RAGBench: the first comprehensive, large-scale RAG benchmark dataset of 100k examples. It covers five unique industry-specific domains and various RAG task types.
description_summary: Evaluates retrieval-augmented generation systems over 100k industry-domain examples using the TRACe metrics (context relevance, utilization, completeness, adherence) rather than a single QA accuracy score.
external_memory_evidence: We sample 100 realistic world knowledge queries from the RAGTruth [ 40 ] QA training set, along with 2,512 unique context document chunks from the same dataset to use as inputs into our mock RAG systems.
task_format_metric: TRACe framework: context relevance, utilization, completeness, adherence (explainable RAG evaluation labels)
example_length: 100–11000 tokens (context token length per RAG example)
what_instead_if_absent: the paper never uses 'long-horizon' or 'long-term'; it frames its scope via standard single-turn RAG (retriever + generator over a domain corpus) with no persistent memory or multi-session structure.
evidence_span: RAG systems are characterized by (1) a document retriever that queries a domain-specific corpus for context information relevant to an input query, and (2) an LLM that generates a response based on the provided query and context.
scope_flag: RAGBench is a generic single-document/single-query RAG evaluation benchmark (context length 100-11k tokens per example) with no cross-session memory, knowledge-update, or long-horizon-execution dimension; it reads as a long-context retrieval benchmark of the kind the charter explicitly places out of scope (akin to NIAH/RULER/LongBench), rather than a persistent-memory or long-horizon-execution benchmark.

description_authors_words: we refer to the CRUD actions that describe interactions between users and knowledge bases and also categorize the range of RAG applications into four distinct types—create, read, update, and delete (CRUD)
description_summary: Chinese-language RAG benchmark evaluating the full retriever+generator pipeline across four knowledge-base interaction types (create/read/update/delete), beyond the question-answering-only scope of most RAG benchmarks.
external_memory_evidence: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique that enhances the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) by incorporating external knowledge sources.
task_format_metric: evaluation across CRUD (create/read/update/delete) RAG application scenarios
what_instead_if_absent: no long-horizon/long-term term appears; the paper concerns comprehensiveness of RAG evaluation across CRUD scenarios, not duration or horizon
evidence_span: this article constructs a large-scale and more comprehensive benchmark and evaluates all the components of RAG systems in various RAG application scenarios.

description_authors_words: We introduce RE-Bench (Research Engineering Benchmark, V1), which consists of 7 challenging, open-ended ML research engineering environments and data from 71 8-hour attempts by 61 distinct human experts.
description_summary: Scores AI agents against human ML-engineering experts on 7 open-ended research-engineering environments under matched multi-hour time budgets, comparing normalized performance.
external_memory_evidence: For each task, the agent (either human or AI) is given a starting solution, access to a machine with 1–6 H100 GPUs, and a way to score their progress.
task_format_metric: normalized score vs human-expert baselines, time-budgeted
example_length: 8 hours (time budget for a single agent run/task attempt) | 29000000 tokens (input tokens consumed per 8-hour agent run)
long_horizon_definition: [contrastive] "time-horizon" refers to the length of time humans spend on the task, used to compare benchmarks by how long a human needs to complete them
evidence_span: Here, “time-horizon” refers to the length of time humans spend on the task.

description_authors_words: Software atomic actions (SWAA): 66 single-step tasks representing short segments of work by software developers, ranging from 1 second to 30 seconds.
description_summary: 66 very short (1-30 second) single-step coding tasks used to anchor the low end of a time-horizon curve measuring how long a task an agent can reliably finish.
task_format_metric: 50% task-completion time horizon (logistic model of success rate vs. human baseline time)
example_length: 1–30 other:seconds (human baseline time to complete the shortest SWAA tasks) | 1–1800 other:minutes (human baseline time to complete HCAST tasks) | 8 hours (fixed human baseline time for RE-Bench tasks (all tasks rated at this length))
long_horizon_definition: [operational-threshold] the paper defines the X%-(task completion) time horizon as 'the length of tasks that models can complete approximately X% of the time,' operationalized via human baseline completion time (e.g. the 50% time horizon is the human-task-duration at which a model succeeds half the time).
evidence_span: we propose tracking AI progress over time using the task completion time horizon: the duration of tasks that models can complete at a certain success probability... we operationalize this by measuring the X%-(task completion) time horizon -the length of tasks that models can complete approximately X% of the time.

description_authors_words: we curate a dataset of over 1200 questions across six domains (e.g., drug dosages, Olympic records, locations) along with content relevant to answering each question... we further apply precise perturbations to the answers in the content
description_summary: 1,200+ QA items with retrieved passages deliberately perturbed to contain wrong answers, measuring whether an LLM adopts the erroneous retrieved content or defends its correct prior belief.
task_format_metric: Accuracy / Prior Bias / Context Bias (conditional-probability metrics)
what_instead_if_absent: the paper never uses 'long-horizon'/'long-term'; it frames the challenge as a single-turn 'clash' between a model's parametric prior response and a retrieved-context response, formally defined via Accuracy/Prior Bias/Context Bias metrics (Sec 3.1), not a duration or session-based construct.
evidence_span: we start with a QA instance x=(q,c) where q is the query and c is the context provided to answer the query. A model's prior response is r(q)... A model's contextual response is r(q|c)

description_authors_words: we introduce BALROG, a novel benchmark designed to assess the agentic capabilities of LLMs and VLMs through a diverse set of challenging games
description_summary: Tests agentic reasoning of LLMs/VLMs across six procedurally-generated game environments (e.g. NetHack, Crafter, BabyAI) of varying difficulty, scored by a standardized 0-100 progression metric.
task_format_metric: fine-grained game-progress metric (% completion) per environment
example_length: 10 turns (turns to complete BabyAI tasks (order of magnitude, 10^1)) | 1000 turns (turns to complete Crafter tasks (order of magnitude, 10^3)) | 10000–100000 turns (turns to complete NetHack tasks (order of magnitude, 10^4-10^5))
long_horizon_definition: [operational-threshold] BALROG characterizes long-horizon-ness via a 'time horizon' table quantifying turns-to-complete per environment, ranging from 10^1 turns (BabyAI) to 10^4-10^5 turns (NetHack), explicitly billing itself as testing 'harder, longer time-horizon interactive settings' than existing benchmarks
evidence_span: Table 1: The tested skills, time horizons, and complexities of interactive decision-making tasks evaluated in BALROG. Compared to existing benchmarks, BALROG provides infrastructure for evaluating model reasoning and decision-making on harder, longer time-horizon interactive settings.

description_authors_words: we present VSI-SUPER, a two-part benchmark: VSR (long-horizon visual spatial recall) and VSC (continual visual spatial counting). These tasks require arbitrarily long video inputs yet are resistant to brute-force context expansion.
description_summary: Two video tasks -- recalling spatial layout after an arbitrarily long tour (VSR) and continually counting objects across a long video stream (VSC) -- designed to resist brute-force long-context scaling.
external_memory_evidence: As new frame arrivs, the oldest frames that exceed the sensory memory window are dequeued and stored in the long-term memory.
task_format_metric: mean relative accuracy (MRA, VSC) + recall accuracy (VSR)
example_length: 10–120 other:minutes (video duration per VSC instance)
long_horizon_definition: [operational-threshold] VSR is named 'long-horizon visual spatial recall' and VSC operationalizes 'long-term consistency' via four explicit video durations: 10, 30, 60, and 120 minutes, with tasks required to handle arbitrarily long video inputs that exceed fixed context windows.
evidence_span: To examine long-term consistency, VSC includes four video durations: 10, 30, 60, and 120 minutes.

description_authors_words: we present an evaluation framework for assessing knowledge conflicts across various dimensions
description_summary: Induces conflicts between a retrieval-augmented LM's parametric memory and retrieved evidence (or among retrieved passages), measuring whether the model trusts its memory, majority evidence, or truth.
external_memory_evidence: RALMs first retrieve a handful of reference evidence from external sources or non-parametric knowledge , and subsequently integrate these external sources with their internal memory for generation.
venue: International Conference on Language Resources and Evaluation
task_format_metric: QA Recall / K-Precision / EM under induced knowledge conflict
what_instead_if_absent: the paper frames its whole topic as 'knowledge conflicts' between an LLM's internal memory and external retrieved evidence, and never uses 'long-horizon' or 'long-term' at all
evidence_span: RALMs will inevitably encounter knowledge conflicts when integrating their internal memory with external sources.

description_authors_words: We construct a benchmark, SafeEdit, which covers nine unsafe categories with various powerful attack prompts and equips comprehensive metrics for systematic evaluation
description_summary: Tests whether a single knowledge-edit applied to detoxify a model actually reduces unsafe outputs across nine attack-prompt categories without degrading general performance.
venue: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
task_format_metric: toxicity/safety metrics across attack prompts before vs. after editing
what_instead_if_absent: no long-horizon/long-term term appears; the paper concerns detoxifying LLMs via one-shot knowledge editing, not duration or horizon
evidence_span: We construct a benchmark, SafeEdit, which covers nine unsafe categories with various powerful attack prompts and equips comprehensive metrics for systematic evaluation.

description_authors_words: we introduce Evo-Memory, a comprehensive streaming benchmark and framework for evaluating self-evolving memory in LLM agents.
description_summary: Streaming benchmark where an LLM agent faces a sequence of tasks and must retrieve, integrate, and update its own memory after each interaction, scored by cumulative accuracy across the stream.
external_memory_evidence: We unify and implement over ten representative memory modules, including retrieval-based, workflow, and hierarchical memory systems, to study their adaptation behavior.
task_format_metric: cumulative accuracy / success & progress rate across sequential task streams (single-turn reasoning + multi-turn embodied)
what_instead_if_absent: the paper repeatedly invokes 'long-term planning', 'long-term assistants', and 'long-horizon experiences' as motivation, but never pins these to a duration/turn-count threshold; it instead operationalizes its scope via 'sequential task streams' across 10 existing datasets that agents must adapt to over test-time evolution.
evidence_span: Statefulness is essential for large language model (LLM) agents to perform long-term planning and problem-solving. This makes memory a critical component, yet its management and evolution remain largely underexplored.

description_authors_words: We introduce SWE-Lancer, a benchmark of over 1,400 freelance software engineering tasks from Upwork, valued at $1 million USD total in real-world payouts.
description_summary: Models resolve real Upwork freelance coding issues and also make SWE-manager proposal choices, with performance converted into the actual dollar payout each task was worth.
external_memory_evidence: Models operate with a basic scaffold that lets them browse the local codebase, modify files, and execute terminal commands.
task_format_metric: end-to-end test pass (IC SWE tasks) + proposal-selection match rate (SWE Manager tasks), mapped to real dollar payouts
example_length: 26 days (time to resolve a task on GitHub (average, Diamond set)) | 69 other:lines_of_code (lines of code modified per IC SWE task (average)) | 2 other:files (files modified per IC SWE task (average))
length_unit_families: retrieved documents; tokens / text length; wall-clock time
what_instead_if_absent: the paper never uses 'long-horizon' to describe task difficulty; its only 'long-term' occurrence concerns economic/labor-market implications of AI-driven software engineering, not benchmark design. Difficulty is instead characterized via real-world resolution time (average 26 days) and monetary payout
evidence_span: AI models with strong real-world software engineering capabilities... could also shift labor demand—especially in the short term for entry-level and freelance software engineers—and have broader long-term implications for the software industry.

description_authors_words: we construct AgentErrorBench, the first dataset of systematically annotated failure trajectories from ALFWorld, GAIA, and WebShop, grounding error analysis in real-world agent rollouts
description_summary: Annotated failure trajectories from ALFWorld, GAIA, and WebShop agent runs, labeled by root-cause error type (memory, reflection, planning, action, system) to localize where multi-step agents break down.
task_format_metric: critical-error-localization accuracy (Step Exact, Step+Module, All-Correct)
what_instead_if_absent: the paper uses 'long-horizon' as an unexamined descriptor of tasks prone to cascading errors, never quantifying a threshold; it instead characterizes trajectory difficulty by where failures cluster (mid-trajectory steps 6-15)
evidence_span: This challenge is especially acute in long-horizon tasks, where early mistakes distort later reasoning and actions, making recovery difficult.

description_authors_words: In this work, we introduce ToT , a novel benchmark for temporal reasoning generated synthetically.
description_summary: Synthetic multiple-choice questions built over generated temporal graphs and event facts, isolating pure temporal-logic and date-arithmetic reasoning from world-knowledge shortcuts.
task_format_metric: multiple-choice/QA accuracy on synthetic temporal-graph questions
example_length: 144.07 other:graph edges (facts) (average number of timestamped-fact edges per synthetic temporal graph (varies by graph-generation algorithm, e.g. Barabasi-Albert))
what_instead_if_absent: the paper frames its topic generically as 'temporal reasoning' and never uses or defines 'long-horizon' or 'long-term'
evidence_span: In this work we focus on temporal reasoning, an essential task for intelligent systems across many domains.

description_authors_words: we introduce the Sequential Diagnosis Benchmark, which transforms 304 diagnostically challenging New England Journal of Medicine clinicopathological conference (NEJM-CPC) cases into stepwise diagnostic encounters.
description_summary: A physician or AI must iteratively request tests and history from a gatekeeper model over 304 hard NEJM case reports, diagnosing under a cost budget for visits and tests ordered.
task_format_metric: diagnostic accuracy + cost of physician visits/tests performed
long_horizon_definition: [contrastive] physicians iteratively formulate and revise diagnostic hypotheses, adapting each subsequent question and test to what they've just learned, and weigh the evolving evidence before committing to a final diagnosis -- contrasted with static vignettes and multiple-choice questions that fail to reflect this iterative process
evidence_span: most evaluations of language models rely on static vignettes and multiple-choice questions that fail to reflect the complexity and nuance of evidence-based medicine in real-world settings... To emulate this iterative process, we introduce the Sequential Diagnosis Benchmark

description_authors_words: We introduce the LongLaMP benchmark consisting of 4 important personalized long-text generation tasks with two settings each.
description_summary: Benchmark of four long-form writing tasks (email, abstract, review, topic writing) where models must generate text personalized to an author's own historical writing samples.
task_format_metric: ROUGE-1/ROUGE-L/METEOR on personalized long-form text generation, conditioned on retrieved user profile
example_length: 85.65 other:profile_items (profile size (average items per user), Email Completion task, User setting) | 191.4 tokens (context length (average tokens retrieved for personalization), Email Completion task) | 92.59 words (output length (average words in the personalized generated text), Email Completion task)
length_unit_families: stored memory items; tokens / text length
what_instead_if_absent: the paper is framed around 'long-text generation' and 'personalization' rather than 'long-horizon'/'long-term'; those specific terms do not appear as the paper's own defining vocabulary in the searched sections
evidence_span: Each researcher has a unique writing style, characterized by factors such as the structure of their arguments, the use of domain-specific language, and the tone they employ making this long-text task challenging.

description_authors_words: we introduce MCP-Universe, the first comprehensive benchmark specifically designed to evaluate LLMs in realistic and hard tasks through interaction with real-world MCP servers
description_summary: Tests LLM agents on realistic long-horizon tasks executed through real-world MCP tool servers across 6 domains (navigation, repo management, finance, 3D design, browser automation, search), graded by execution-based evaluators.
task_format_metric: execution-based success rate (SR) + average evaluator score (AE) + average steps (AS)
example_length: 4.82–8.22 steps (average number of interaction steps per successful task (varies by model, 4.82-8.22))
what_instead_if_absent: the paper lists 'long-horizon multi-turn tool calls' as one of several 'realistic challenges' (alongside long context windows, scattered evidence, large tool spaces) that its benchmark captures, but never states a step-count or duration threshold defining what makes a task long-horizon; the closest quantification is the average-steps-per-task (AS) execution metric, e.g. 4.82-8.22 steps for successful runs.
evidence_span: existing benchmarks are overly simplistic and fail to capture real application challenges such as long-horizon reasoning and large, unfamiliar tool spaces.

benchmark_name: SCM evaluation dataset (long-term dialogues, book summarization, meeting summarization)
description_authors_words: we annotate a dataset to evaluate the effectiveness of SCM for handling lengthy inputs. The annotated dataset covers three tasks: long-term dialogues, book summarization, and meeting summarization.
description_summary: Dataset for evaluating long-input handling across three tasks -- long-term dialogue, book summarization, and meeting summarization -- used to test a memory-stream agent's retrieval over long history.
external_memory_evidence: The memory stream stores all historical memory items and can easily achieve high-speed access through cache storage technologies such as Redis or vector databases like Pinecone
venue: International Conference on Database Systems for Advanced Applications
task_format_metric: answer accuracy + memory retrieval recall + single-turn/multi-turn accuracy
example_length: 20000–2000000 tokens (tokens per instance across the annotated evaluation dataset (long-term dialogues, book and meeting summarization)) | 100 turns (turns since a topic was last discussed, in the illustrative long-term dialogue example)
long_horizon_definition: [contrastive] each input segment is processed using two types of memory: 'a long-term memory (activation memory) that retains historical information and a short-term memory (flash memory) that captures real-time memory information from the preceding segment' -- long-term memory is defined by contrast with short-term/flash memory as the component retaining information across all past segments rather than just the immediately preceding one.
evidence_span: Each segment is processed by the LLM using two types of memory: a long-term memory (activation memory) that retains historical information and a short-term memory (flash memory) that captures real-time memory information from the preceding segment.

description_authors_words: we construct a Knowledge-oriented LLM Assessment benchmark (KoLA), in which we carefully design three crucial factors...
description_summary: Tests LLM world knowledge across a four-level cognitive taxonomy (memorization, understanding, applying, creating) using Wikipedia plus continuously refreshed corpora, scored with contrastive standardized metrics.
external_memory_evidence: In the evaluation of the KA level, a notable phenomenon is that knowledge graph (KG)-based reasoning question answering tasks are almost impossible to complete without the use of KG.
task_format_metric: standardized scores across four cognitive levels (Memorization, Understanding, Applying, Creating), self-contrast knowledge-creation metric
what_instead_if_absent: the paper never uses 'long-horizon' or 'long-term' for its own construct (the sole occurrence of 'long-term' in the text is a supporter-acknowledgment sentence unrelated to the benchmark); it frames its temporal-evolution scope via a quarterly-updated 'evolving data' split versus a static 'known data' split.
evidence_span: The KoLA dataset will be updated every three months to provide timely references for developing LLMs and knowledge systems.

description_authors_words: we introduce EgoLifeQA, a suite of long-context, life-oriented question-answering tasks designed to provide meaningful assistance in daily life by addressing practical questions as recalling past relevant events, monitoring health and offering personalized recommendations
description_summary: Multiple-choice QA grounded in a week of continuous first-person video/audio from six cohabiting people, requiring recall of past events across hundreds of hours of egocentric footage.
external_memory_evidence: In the first stage, EgoRAG integrates with EgoGPT to extract video clip captions and store them in a structured memory module, ensuring efficient retrieval of time-stamped contextual information.
task_format_metric: multiple-choice QA accuracy over ultra-long-context egocentric video/audio
example_length: 2–24 hours (certification length (look-back time needed to answer a question)) | 300 hours (total egocentric video dataset duration (EgoLife Dataset, across 6 participants))
long_horizon_definition: [operational-threshold] the paper operationalizes 'long-term'/'ultra-long-context' via 'certification length' -- the look-back time needed to retrieve the evidence for an answer -- stratified into four levels ranging from 2 hours to 24 hours; during annotation, only questions requiring information from at least 5 minutes prior were retained at all
evidence_span: Annotators also generated distractors for multiple-choice questions... and specified the look-back time (certification length) necessary for retrieving the correct answer... brightness levels reflecting 4-level certification length [11] (from 2h to 24h).

description_authors_words: we introduce DISCOVERYWORLD, the first virtual environment for developing and benchmarking an agent's ability to perform complete cycles of novel scientific discovery.
description_summary: Text-based virtual environment with 120 tasks across 8 science topics where an agent forms hypotheses, runs experiments, and reports conclusions, scored by completion and correctness.
task_format_metric: task completion + task process + explanatory knowledge discovery scores
example_length: 100 steps (maximum steps per task (Easy difficulty)) | 1000 steps (maximum steps per task (Normal/Challenge difficulty))
long_horizon_definition: [explicit-stated] DiscoveryWorld tasks are long-horizon because they require multiple facets of discovery (ideation, experimentation, systematic search, and analysis) to be performed to solve a task
evidence_span: DiscoveryWorld tasks are long-horizon, requiring multiple facets of discovery including ideation, experimentation, systematic search, and analysis to be performed to solve a task.

description_authors_words: We introduce AucArena, a novel evaluation suite that simulates auctions, a setting chosen for being highly unpredictable and involving many skills related to resource and risk management, while also being easy to evaluate.
description_summary: LLM agents bid against each other across sequential ascending-price auctions with fixed budgets, testing strategic planning, budget management, and goal adherence under competitive uncertainty.
external_memory_evidence: Context length restrictions prevent the inclusion of full bidding and conversation histories into LLMs. To compensate, we use a summarized dynamic memory of the auction’s state
task_format_metric: Profit / TrueSkill ranking under sequential ascending-price auctions
example_length: 10 other:items (items presented sequentially per auction game by default (2 items at each of 5 starting price tiers, $1,000-$5,000))
what_instead_if_absent: 'long-term planning'/'long-term sequential auctions'/'long-term objectives' recur as unexamined given descriptors of the setting, without a stated round-count or duration threshold; the paper's own concrete anchor is the default auction structure of 10 sequential items
evidence_span: Bidder agents engage in long-term sequential auctions with a fixed budget, allowing for strategic considerations.

description_authors_words: we curate EditEverything, a new benchmark for long-form knowledge in diverse formats
description_summary: Model-editing test set of long-form, multi-domain knowledge (math, code, chemistry, news, poetry) up to 458 tokens, checking whether edits generalize across original, paraphrased, and sub-questions via BERTScore/ROUGE similarity.
task_format_metric: editing accuracy/efficacy on long-form, diverse-formatted knowledge (poetry, code, math), vs. baseline editors
example_length: 458–458 tokens (tokens per knowledge-edit target sequence in EditEverything (maximum, vs. 156-token max in prior benchmark AKEW))
what_instead_if_absent: the paper never uses 'long-horizon' or 'long-term'; its central axis of difficulty is 'long-form' KNOWLEDGE (token length of the fact/content being edited, e.g. code, poetry, math), not a duration/session-based construct
evidence_span: Current model editing methods, however, struggle with long-form knowledge in diverse formats, such as poetry, code snippets, and mathematical derivations.

description_authors_words: Our benchmarks allow for the development of algorithms that enable LLMs to interact with an environment to achieve long-term objectives, by providing tasks with online simulators and offline datasets.
description_summary: Suite of 8 multi-turn text-based tasks (e.g. persuasion dialogue, guessing games, mazes) with online simulators, used to train and score RL algorithms on goal-directed multi-turn language interaction.
task_format_metric: Normalized reward / average return across 8 RL and dialogue tasks
example_length: 19.7 turns (average trajectory length, in agent responses, for the Maze task (Table 1)) | 46.7 turns (average trajectory length, in agent responses, for the Chess task (Table 1))
what_instead_if_absent: 'long-term objective' is used as an unexamined given contrasted against standard supervised-learning tasks, without a stated turn-count or duration threshold; the paper's own concrete anchor is Table 1's per-task 'avg length' statistic (in agent-response units), which varies widely by task (e.g. 4.82 for Wordle vs. 46.7 for Chess)
evidence_span: these are often supervised learning tasks that do not test the LLMs' abilities to achieve a specific long-term objective.

description_authors_words: proposing (i) RAMDocs (Retrieval with Ambiguity and Misinformation in Documents), a new dataset that simulates complex and realistic scenarios for conflicting evidence for a user query, including ambiguity, misinformation, and noise
description_summary: RAG systems answer ambiguous queries over retrieved documents that simultaneously contain conflicting misinformation, noise, and multiple valid answers, without being misled.
task_format_metric: exact match (EM), correctly selecting valid answers over misinformation-supported ones
