venue: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
task_format_metric: Edit success (ES), locality (L), portability (P), harmonic mean (HM)
example_length: 2 steps (edits per composite-reasoning CRAFT instance, treated as two separate time steps)
what_instead_if_absent: the paper frames its dataset around 'real-time'/'ever-evolving' knowledge rather than 'long-horizon'/'long-term'; those exact terms are not used to characterize the setting
evidence_span: we introduce CRAFT, an ever-evolving real-world dataset for knowledge editing... We hope this work may serve as a catalyst for shifting the focus of knowledge editing from static update to dynamic evolution.

description_authors_words: we present a systematic evaluation of seven frontier models on 36 long-horizon tasks based on a new framework that uses rule-based metrics to characterize within-run behavior through Solution Framing, Execution, and Feedback Control and controlled comparisons to assess experience reuse within and across tasks.
description_summary: Not a fixed benchmark artifact: a process-level evaluation framework for long-horizon AI R&D agents scoring solution framing, execution, and feedback control, plus whether experience transfers across repeated attempts on the same 36 tasks.
external_memory_evidence: In the without-experience condition, we re-initialize the agent and erase its prior context, on-disk notes, and in-code comments while preserving the solution at the branch point.
task_format_metric: Rule-based process diagnostics (Solution Framing/Execution/Feedback-Control scores) plus final avg@3/best@3 task score
example_length: 2–12 hours (per-task wall-clock budget, determined by workload scale)
what_instead_if_absent: 'long-horizon' is used repeatedly as an unexamined given describing the auto-research/experimentation setting, without ever being pinned to a definition, threshold, or contrast
evidence_span: Autonomous agents are increasingly capable of improving models, systems, and other technical artifacts through long-horizon experimentation.

description_authors_words: we introduce M3Eval, the first comprehensive evaluation framework and benchmark for probing different memory dimensions in multi-modal models. Grounded in cognitive psychology, our design features carefully constructed tasks that isolate key aspects of memory
description_summary: Cognitively-grounded video tasks isolate specific memory dimensions in multimodal models -- divided attention across parallel streams, interference, interleaved-event recall, and N-back -- rather than testing perception or reasoning in general.
task_format_metric: Multiple-choice/QA accuracy across divided-attention, interference, interleaved-events and N-Back sub-tasks
example_length: 53.6 other:minutes (average duration of the source videos used per question (403 hours across 451 videos))
what_instead_if_absent: the paper frames its contribution around cognitively-grounded 'memory' evaluation (divided attention, interference, source memory) rather than defining 'long-horizon' or 'long-term'; those terms appear only in citations to other benchmarks (Mem-gallery, LongMemEval, etc.) in related work
evidence_span: Mem-gallery: benchmarking multimodal long-term conversational memory for mllm agents .

description_authors_words: we introduce SeqMem-Eval, a diagnostic evaluation framework for sequentially evolving LLM memory.
description_summary: Evaluation harness (not a fixed dataset) that scores external, prompt-mediated memory across sequential tasks on online utility, hold-out generalization, backward transfer, and forgetting, showing high final accuracy can hide poor memory quality.
external_memory_evidence: At each step, the model maintains a memory state M t M_{t} , which may contain raw trajectories, retrieved examples, summaries, workflows, reflections, or other forms of accumulated experience from previous interactions.
task_format_metric: Online accuracy trajectory, hold-out generalization, backward transfer (BWT), forgetting, and efficiency (tokens/runtime)
example_length: 132–1170 tasks (tasks per sequential online stream (T), across constituent datasets)
long_horizon_definition: [explicit-stated] an LLM interacts with a stream of tasks and maintains an external memory that is updated over time, formalized as an online task sequence D={(x_tau,y_tau)}_{tau=1}^{T} with evolving memory states {M_t}_{t=1}^{T}
evidence_span: we consider a sequentially evolving memory setting, where an LLM interacts with a stream of tasks and maintains an external memory that is updated over time.

description_authors_words: we introduce a decoupled evaluation paradigm that administers paired Know and Act tests to the same user preference.
description_summary: Separates whether an agent merely recalls a user preference from whether it actually acts on it in a matching behavioral scenario, testing 1,000 preferences at three expression strengths across 16 memory systems.
external_memory_evidence: we feed conversation chunks to memory systems one at a time using a standardized memorization template (Appendix  B.1 ). This ensures that each system processes information through its native mechanisms: Mem0  ( Chhikara et al., 2025 ) performs fact extraction, Letta  ( Packer et al., 2024 ) manages hierarchical memory tiers, and knowledge-graph-based systems construct their graphs progressively.
task_format_metric: Know Accuracy, Act Accuracy, and Utilization Rate across 16 memory systems
example_length: 79.7–116 other:chunks (conversation chunks per persona chunk-sequence) | 27500 tokens (tokens per persona sequence (explicit-expression condition; incidental condition averages ~33.1K))
long_horizon_definition: [explicit-stated] LLM agents are becoming 'personalized long-term companions capable of sustained interaction with users over days, weeks, and months', with memory as the core capability enabling this
evidence_span: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are rapidly evolving from stateless tools into personalized long-term companions capable of sustained interaction with users over days, weeks, and months

description_authors_words: LifecycleBench is a temporal disambiguation benchmark in which the correct answer depends on lifecycle state. It comprises 516 questions over 40 synthetic personas, each with ~35 multi-session conversations spanning 18 simulated months, structured into nine attack vectors
description_summary: 516 temporal-disambiguation questions over 40 synthetic personas (18 simulated months, 9 attack vectors like superseded preferences and selective forgetting), testing whether a memory system tracks which stored fact is currently valid rather than merely retrieving any matching fact.
task_format_metric: Pass rate (LLM-judge correctness) and confabulation rate on temporal-disambiguation QA
example_length: 35 sessions (sessions per persona bank) | 17.4–18.53 months (simulated months spanned per persona (mean; range 14.95-18.53))
what_instead_if_absent: the paper positions its own contribution around 'lifecycle management' (which memories should persist, be replaced, or expire) rather than defining 'long-horizon'/'long-term'; those terms appear only when characterizing OTHER benchmarks (LongMemEval, LoCoMo) in related work
evidence_span: LongMemEval and LoCoMo measure long-horizon retrieval without testing whether a system distinguishes current from outdated state... We therefore position LifecycleBench not as the first benchmark to touch temporal updates or forgetting but as a dense lifecycle stress test

description_authors_words: we introduce Cutverse, a benchmark designed to systematically evaluate autonomous GUI agents in realistic media post-production environments.
description_summary: 186 long-horizon media-editing tasks across 7 professional creative apps (Premiere Pro, Photoshop) test whether a GUI agent executes dense, tightly coupled interaction sequences in authentic post-production workflows.
task_format_metric: Task success rate via Milestone-driven QA evaluator (post-hoc VLM-as-judge)
example_length: 18.73–239 steps (steps per trajectory (average, across all 186 tasks))
long_horizon_definition: [operational-threshold] 'long-horizon complexity' is quantified as trajectory step count: averaging 18.73 steps per trajectory with a severe long-tail distribution reaching a peak of 239 steps, stratified into a Low-to-Extreme complexity spectrum
evidence_span: The dataset exhibits a severe long-tail distribution, averaging 18.73 steps per trajectory—substantially surpassing standard web-navigation benchmarks—with peak execution horizons reaching 239 steps.

description_authors_words: We introduce AcademiClaw, a bilingual benchmark of 80 complex, long-horizon tasks sourced directly from university students' real academic workflows -- homework, research projects, competitions, and personal projects -- that they found current AI agents unable to solve effectively.
description_summary: Agents attempt 80 real, hard academic tasks (contributed by students who found current AI unable to solve them) spanning math, linguistics, GPU-based RL, and system debugging, each scored in an isolated sandbox by multi-method rubrics.
task_format_metric: Rubric-based pass rate (score>=75 of 100) and average score, six-method scoring rubric
example_length: 33–136 actions (average tool calls per task) | 11.7–40 other:minutes (mean agent execution (wall-clock) time per task)
long_horizon_definition: [operational-threshold] long-horizon tasks are characterized empirically by the agent trajectories they induce: an average of 33 tool calls per task (up to 136 for the most complex), a mean execution time of 11.7 minutes and a maximum exceeding 40 minutes, reflecting extended chains of reading, coding, debugging, and verification
evidence_span: agents invoke an average of 33 tool calls per task (up to 136 for the most complex ones), with a mean execution time of 11.7 minutes and a maximum exceeding 40 minutes, reflecting extended chains of reading, coding, debugging, and verification.

description_authors_words: we introduce ATOD, a benchmark and synthetic dialogue generation pipeline that produces richly annotated conversations requiring long-term reasoning. ATOD captures key characteristics of advanced TOD, including multi-goal coordination, dependency management, memory, adaptability, and proactivity.
description_summary: Synthetic task-oriented dialogues requiring an agent to coordinate multiple interleaved goals with dependencies over long-horizon context, scored on goal detection, status tracking, and dependency-aware completion.
task_format_metric: Goal Detection Accuracy, Status Tracking Accuracy, Dependency-Aware Goal Completion Rate (dGCR), Turns to Completion
example_length: 54 turns (average turns per dialogue in ATOD (Table 2))
long_horizon_definition: [explicit-stated] Long-Horizon Memory is explicitly listed as one of the paper's key characteristics: 'Goals can span many turns, requiring consistent state tracking and dependency management over extended interactions'
evidence_span: Long-Horizon Memory. Goals can span many turns, requiring consistent state tracking and dependency management over extended interactions;

description_authors_words: We introduce StaminaBench, a benchmark that measures the stamina of coding agents: how many consecutive interaction turns (change requests) they can handle before failing.
description_summary: Tests how many consecutive follow-up change requests (up to 100) a coding agent can correctly implement on a REST API server before failing, rather than measuring fraction of one-shot tasks solved.
external_memory_evidence: For storing the data, the server must use any database solution you’d like
task_format_metric: Average turns passed (stamina) and end-to-end pass rate @R (retry budget)
example_length: 100 turns (consecutive interaction turns (change requests) per scenario)
long_horizon_definition: [explicit-stated] the paper explicitly defines its scope term: 'we use "multi-turn" to denote multiple interaction turns between the user and the agent, not the internal tool-use steps the agent takes within a single user request', and frames long-horizon-ness as sessions that 'run dozens or hundreds of turns' unlike prior benchmarks with 'very low' turn counts
evidence_span: In this work, we use “multi-turn” to denote multiple interaction turns between the user and the agent, not the internal tool-use steps the agent takes within a single user request.

description_authors_words: We introduce FORESIGHT-9, a prospective and process-aware benchmark built from nine auditable counterfactual stress worldlines branching from a common July 2026 information boundary.
description_summary: Nine counterfactual future 'worldlines' of staged macro-financial events branching from a fixed information boundary, testing a trading agent's live long-horizon adaptation and internal process consistency rather than backtested historical returns.
external_memory_evidence:
Account state, the
per-cycle factor-library audit trail, research memory, and the evolving
workspace are all released artifacts.
task_format_metric: Prospective NAV/returns vs. simple non-learning controls; process-audit metrics of research/decision/portfolio-state consistency
example_length: 2468 days (daily marks per worldline (from the 2026-07-16 shared anchor through 2035-12-31))
long_horizon_definition: [operational-threshold] the paper's '36 long-horizon runs' are each a worldline spanning from the shared 2026-07-16 anchor through 2035-12-31 (~2,468 daily marks, roughly 9.5 years), which is the concrete span the term 'long-horizon' is attached to
evidence_span: the synthetic worldlines diverge from 2026-07-17 through 2035-12-31 ( ∼2,468 daily marks).

description_authors_words: We also introduce TimelyQABench, the first benchmark for regulation-heavy domains with overlapping-evolving challenges.
description_summary: Tests retrieval-augmented QA over legal and regulatory documents where amendments overlap and override only parts of earlier clauses, requiring temporal-distance-aware ranking to retrieve the version-appropriate text.
external_memory_evidence: TimelyQABench , the first benchmark centered on regulatory corpora with successive amendments; and experiments showing that TimelyRAG improves retrieval by up to +28.6% in nDCG@10 and +19.1% in Hit@10 across retrieval methods.
task_format_metric: Retrieval nDCG@5/@10 and downstream QA accuracy on time-sensitive queries
example_length: 3.1 other:passages (passages required to derive a correct answer per query (average, across TimelyQABench domains))
what_instead_if_absent: the paper never uses 'long-horizon' or 'long-term'; it frames its temporal challenge entirely around 'time-critical'/'time-sensitive' retrieval over 'overlapping-evolving' documents, defining six specific temporal-reasoning categories (exemptions, amendments, validity periods, event-based conditions, version overrides, scope restrictions) instead
evidence_span: Within these domains, we define six categories in Table 1, covering common temporal reasoning requirements such as exemptions, amendments, validity periods, event-based conditions, version overrides, and scope restrictions.

description_authors_words: We construct a benchmark and evaluation protocol that separately assesses whether memory contains gap-resolving evidence and whether the generated summary reflects it
description_summary: Streaming dialogue summarization over histories up to 160K tokens tests whether a bounded memory recovers the specific earlier evidence a current summarization window presupposes, separate from summary fluency.
external_memory_evidence: We propose ReMEMBER, a missing-evidence memory framework that conditions retrieval on unresolved window dependencies and refines retrieved chunks into evidence-dense memory under a fixed budget.
task_format_metric: Memory recall (gap-resolving evidence coverage) and gap-resolution completeness / summary-quality composite score
example_length: 7000–160000 tokens (prior-history length (H_t) available per instance)
what_instead_if_absent: the paper uses 'long-term dialogue histories' once as an unexamined given in its opening framing sentence, then substitutes a precisely defined and named task, 'streaming dialogue summarization', operationalized via token-length windows and histories (1,024-token windows; histories from 7K to 160K tokens)
evidence_span: Streaming dialogue summarization requires utterance-level grounding over long-term dialogue histories, which existing dialogue summarization benchmarks generally lack.

description_authors_words: we introduce LongEvoRoleBench, which pairs four long-dialogue corpora for cross-episode evolution with four short-dialogue corpora as within-scene state-tracking checks, under a unified next-utterance protocol.
description_summary: Four long-dialogue and four short-dialogue role-play corpora under a unified next-utterance protocol, testing whether a model's generated character speech reflects the character's currently evolved state rather than just a static persona or bare memory recall.
external_memory_evidence: This baseline state is the starting point: the session and moment strata must be updated to track developments within each scene, and the persona stratum evolves across episodes as the character undergoes lasting change.
task_format_metric: Character/Semantic/Embedding LLM-judge and cosine-similarity scores on next-utterance generation
example_length: 7–10 other:seasons (TV seasons/episode-run spanned per tracked character in the long-dialogue corpora (Star Trek 7, The Office 9, Friends 10))
long_horizon_definition: [contrastive] the benchmark explicitly pairs four long-dialogue corpora (Friends, The Office, Harry Potter, Star Trek -- each grouped into a season-episode-scene hierarchy, tracking cross-episode persona evolution) against four short-dialogue corpora (RAIDEN, CharacterEval, SimsConv, ChatHaruhi -- single-scene, within-scene state-tracking checks only), operationalizing 'long-horizon' as the long-dialogue side of this explicit split
evidence_span: LongEvoRoleBench...pairs four long-dialogue corpora for cross-episode evolution with four short-dialogue corpora as within-scene state-tracking checks, under a unified next-utterance protocol.

description_authors_words: we introduce MedClawBench, a de-leaked, doctor-grounded benchmark of 1,123 questions over self-built long neurosurge...
description_summary: Tests whether an agent answers before/after/across-stage questions about tens-of-minutes surgical videos by grounding each answer in visual evidence retrieved from specific points across the procedure, not a compressed whole-video summary.
external_memory_evidence: the orchestrator is backed by an external knowledge base queried via RAG and by a library of tunable skills derived from past failures.
task_format_metric: Four-dimension LLM-judge reward average (1-5 scale) on visual-temporal/visual-perception questions
example_length: 28.5 other:minutes (median surgical source-video duration per question)
long_horizon_definition: [explicit-stated] We call this ability, grounding a question about the temporal evolution of a whole procedure in the visual evidence itself, long-horizon temporal reasoning
evidence_span: We call this ability, grounding a question about the temporal evolution of a whole procedure in the visual evidence itself, long-horizon temporal reasoning.

aliases: BioAgent Bench (external comparison benchmark, reused not authored here)
description_authors_words: The agent must explore task data, construct or adapt an executable workflow DAG, bind inputs and dataset collections, monitor execution, debug failures, and validate biological outputs
description_summary: Held-out, peer-reviewed Galaxy bioinformatics workflows (build DAGs, bind datasets, debug execution, validate biological correctness) testing whether a coding agent's accumulated tactic library improves long-horizon workflow completion versus no-memory or reflection-only baselines.
external_memory_evidence: Figure 1: Overview of Process-Reward Tactic Evolution. Training executes curriculum-organized Galaxy rollouts, scores them with process rewards, and updates an external tactic state. Inference retrieves the trained tactic library for isolated workers executing held-out Galaxy workflow tasks.
task_format_metric: weighted final score = 0.6*Workflow-completion + 0.4*Biological-correctness, plus token/API-round/execution-time efficiency
example_length: 11.34 steps (average workflow-graph dependency-chain depth per task (test35 held-out split)) | 13.0 other:tools (average number of distinct Galaxy tools used per task (test35 held-out split))
long_horizon_definition: [contrastive] long-horizon here means a task is solved only when the agent builds, imports, runs, repairs, and validates an executable workflow through a real software backend across many dependent steps, in contrast to short-answer biomedical QA which requires only a single textual answer
evidence_span: Unlike short-answer biomedical QA, a Galaxy task is solved only when the agent builds, imports, runs, repairs, and validates a workflow through a real software backend.

description_authors_words: OSWorkerBench Benchmark and Insights: A benchmark of 100 long-horizon office tasks across 41 applications that supports instruction-only and demonstration-guided evaluation.
description_summary: 100 long-horizon office tasks across 41 real applications test a GUI agent under instruction-only versus demonstration-guided settings, scored by strict success and partial-credit progress.
task_format_metric: strict task success rate + progress score (partial-credit), under instruction-only and demonstration-guided evaluation modes
example_length: 100 turns (average observation-to-action decision turns per task for a capable model (Kimi-2.6) under instruction-only evaluation, on the 45-task variant-demo (deliberately long-horizon) subset) | 200 steps (maximum interaction-step budget allowed per task across all agents)
long_horizon_definition: [explicit-stated] Long-Memory tasks require delayed reuse of dynamic information or sustained tracking of constraints and workflow state (as opposed to Multi-App tasks, which require information transfer across applications); OSWorkerBench separately annotates 67 of its 100 tasks as Long-Memory on this basis
evidence_span: 67 Long-Memory tasks require delayed reuse of dynamic information, while 49 Multi-App tasks require substantive information transfer across at least three applications.

description_authors_words: we construct EvoSkillBench, a benchmark dataset of malicious interaction trajectories for inducing malicious skill formation in self-evolving agents, and introduce EvoSkillSafetyBench, a post-attack benchmark for evaluating whether injected malicious skills are subsequently retrieved and activated as harmful behaviors.
description_summary: Red-teams self-evolving agents' skill-generation pipelines by injecting malicious interaction trajectories, then tests whether the resulting harmful 'skills' get stored and later retrieved and re-activated as normal behavior.
external_memory_evidence: An attack succeeds only when the malicious capability is persistently stored as a reusable skill, rather than merely generating a transient harmful response.
task_format_metric: attack success rate (pass@k over iterative attack loops) for skill-injection; downstream retrieval/activation rate for EvoSkillSafetyBench
example_length: 3 turns (turns per EvoSkillBench interaction trajectory (fixed user-assistant-user structure: 2 user turns + 1 assistant turn)) | 4 other:attack-loop-iterations (maximum iterative attack-loop attempts (k) allowed per benchmark instance in the pass@k protocol)
what_instead_if_absent: the paper uses 'long-horizon' and 'long-term' only as unexamined descriptors of why skill-based architectures matter generally ('persistent capability accumulation and long-term performance improvement', 'skill-based architectures ... for long-horizon task execution'), never defining what makes a task or trajectory long-horizon within its own benchmark
evidence_span: Recent LLM-based agents increasingly adopt skill-based architectures that store and retrieve reusable capabilities for long-horizon task execution and capability reuse

description_authors_words: We address this with MNIST-PRO, a benchmark that isolates agentic perception by converting MNIST digit recognition into a sequential, glimpse-based search task with lookback constraints.
description_summary: Converts MNIST digit recognition into a sequential glimpse-based search under partial observability, isolating whether an agent builds and revises a coherent perceptual working-memory state from fragmentary visual observations.
external_memory_evidence: We evaluate ten multimodal models across four memory representations, including raw visual history, textual states, structured metric grid maps, and a consolidated visual canvas.
task_format_metric: digit-recognition accuracy (Level 1 single-digit, Level 2 multi-digit) + average step count to prediction
example_length: 5.74–5.74 steps (average glimpse/exploration steps per episode before prediction, Level 1 (single-digit), across representative models) | 13.99–13.99 steps (average glimpse/exploration steps per episode before prediction, Level 2 (multi-digit), across representative models)
what_instead_if_absent: the paper uses 'long-horizon' only in passing ('long-horizon search') to describe one of the capabilities its two difficulty levels are meant to stress, and instead formalizes a controllable 'task horizon' (episode length under a POMDP) as an experimental knob without ever pinning down what counts as long
evidence_span: The two levels are designed to progressively test spatial tracking, visual integration, long-horizon search, and sequential memory.

aliases: MuMu-QA long-dialogue split; MuMu-QA ultra-long stress split
description_authors_words: we introduce MuMu-QA, a benchmark for multi-turn multi-hop RAG with explicit cross-turn sub-question dependency annotations
description_summary: Tests multi-turn, multi-hop conversational RAG by requiring a system to track sub-question-level reasoning dependencies across turns, not just raw dialogue history, scored by turn-level exact-match/F1 against gold answers.
external_memory_evidence: this design externalizes conversational state from the answering model, which remains stateless while the recurrent state and trace DAG jointly maintain local and long-range conversational memory.
task_format_metric: turn-level Exact Match / F1 against gold answers, plus GoldCtx recall and retrieved-paragraph-count efficiency
example_length: 12.17–32 turns (average turns per dialogue, long-dialogue split (train; main evaluation split, range 6-32)) | 52.93–67 turns (average turns per dialogue, ultra-long stress-test split (range 33-67))
long_horizon_definition: [operational-threshold] MuMu-QA distinguishes a short-dialogue split (3-7 turns), a main long-dialogue split (6-32 turns, avg. 12.17 in training) used for the primary evaluation, and an ultra-long stress-test split (33-67 turns, avg. 52.93) constructed by interleaving multiple topic-related sessions specifically to exceed the dialogue lengths seen during training
evidence_span: We further construct long dialogues by interleaving topic-related sessions, producing conversations of up to several dozen turns for training and evaluation.

description_authors_words: we investigate how different memory architectures behave when EQA agents are evaluated sequentially, with multiple questions answered in the same scene while memory is carried forward across queries.
description_summary: Same embodied-QA scene answered across a sequence of questions with memory carried forward between them (rather than resetting per episode), testing whether an agent's memory architecture retains reusable visual-semantic evidence, not just where it explored.
external_memory_evidence: we highlight the necessity of structured, spatially grounded memory: architectures that map persistent visual observations onto metric 3D geometry preserve visual-semantic evidence in a coherent scene representation.
task_format_metric: per-query-index answer score (1-5) and navigation time, comparing episodic vs. sequential (memory-persisting) evaluation of the same agent
example_length: 10–13 tasks (questions per scene-level sequence in the sequentialized OpenEQA benchmark (majority of scenes; over 60% of scenes have at least 10))
long_horizon_definition: [contrastive] long-horizon/sequential operation is defined by contrast with the episodic formulation: in episodic EQA each question is an independent task and the agent's internal state is reset between episodes, whereas sequential (long-horizon) EQA requires memory to persist across multiple, temporally linked queries in the same scene so that knowledge acquired from prior interactions is reused rather than re-explored from scratch
evidence_span: it remains unclear whether these architectures encode environmental knowledge in a form that supports long-horizon reuse, or whether they primarily function as short-term navigation aids

description_authors_words: We introduce a behavioral evaluation framework that calibrates TTT memory claims to the evidence that supports them.
description_summary: Not a benchmark itself: a methodology paper giving an evidence ladder and matched-baseline protocol to test whether test-time-training claims of deployed memory or personalization are backed by real later recall, not just proxy metrics like perplexity.
external_memory_evidence: The BM25-style retrieval baseline builds a fixed memory bank whose retrieval unit is the support sentence.
task_format_metric: position/methodology paper: a claim-calibrated evidence ladder (S/B/D levels) plus a matched-baseline evaluation protocol, validated by auditing ~24 coded TTT papers and by a small controlled nonce-fact LoRA diagnostic (loss vs. free-form recall)
what_instead_if_absent: the paper never itself defines 'long-term' or 'long-horizon' by duration/session-count; 'long-term'/'very long-term' appear only inside citations to OTHER benchmarks it audits (LoCoMo = 'very long-term conversational memory', LongMemEval = 'long-term interactive memory', Mem2ActBench = 'long-term memory utilization'). In place of a duration-based definition, the paper substitutes a directness-of-evidence framework: whether reported evaluation shows later recall, paraphrase robustness, retention, locality, and conflict handling after the original support context is removed
evidence_span: LoCoMo [ 18 ] evaluates very long-term conversational memory; LongMemEval [ 31 ] benchmarks long-term interactive memory in chat assistants
scope_flag: The paper's primary contribution is an evaluation methodology/taxonomy (the evidence ladder) for judging OTHER work's memory claims, not a benchmark artifact with its own released examples; the one original experiment (a nonce-fact LoRA diagnostic) is a small internal case study, not a shipped dataset. Included here because it directly theorizes what would count as genuine long-term/deployment memory evidence, which is squarely on-topic for this catalog even without a named artifact.

description_authors_words: we also introduce MemoryQuest, a challenging multi-session benchmark in which each query is annotated with 3-5 dated reference facts subject to a low query-reference similarity constraint
description_summary: 1,625 multi-session queries, each needing 3-5 dated reference facts that deliberately have low embedding similarity to the query, testing whether retrieval finds relevant facts dense retrieval alone would miss.
external_memory_evidence: The memory store maintains the agent’s knowledge of the user across sessions. PGR is agnostic to the underlying storage technology and requires only a queryable memory interface; the backend may be a vector index, a knowledge graph, or a hybrid store.
task_format_metric: retrieval recall of required reference facts + LLM-judge/human win-rate on response quality
example_length: 77.6 sessions (average sessions per user history in MemoryQuest) | 6.2 turns (average exchanges per session in MemoryQuest) | 5–30 turns (turns per individual multi-turn conversation expanded from a timeline event)
long_horizon_definition: [explicit-stated] requires dialogue assistants to retrieve user-specific facts from extended interaction histories
evidence_span: Long-horizon personalization requires dialogue assistants to retrieve user-specific facts from extended interaction histories.

description_authors_words: We introduce APIFlow-Bench, a fully auditable benchmark for long-horizon, dependent REST-API workflows that decomposes performance into seven engineering capabilities and requires agents to produce answers supported by the actual call path.
description_summary: Synthetic long, dependent REST-API workflows (44,362 execution transcripts) with deterministic, provenance-checked grading that traces a canary value through the real call chain, testing whether an agent's answer is actually backed by its executed API calls rather than just completing the workflow.
task_format_metric: deterministic provenance-checked task success (state check + typed answer-card verification), pass@k and all-k-of-k reliability
example_length: 1–20 steps (subtasks per dependent API workflow chain (solo=1 up to clean 20-subtask chains, the paper's long condition))
long_horizon_definition: [contrastive] long-horizon tasks reveal failure modes hidden by short, independently sampled instances; the paper operationalizes this by growing dependent subtasks forward within the same API world so that chain length varies independently of tool surface or task distribution
evidence_span: Long-horizon tasks reveal failure modes that are often hidden by short, independently sampled instances. τ-bench's pass k evaluates the probability that all k independent executions succeed, not whether a single execution does.

description_authors_words: we design StratMem-Bench, a new benchmark to evaluate strategic memory use in character-centric dialogues. This dataset comprises 657 instances where virtual characters must navigate heterogeneous memory pools containing required, supportive, and irrelevant memories.
description_summary: Tests whether a virtual character actively selects and deploys the right memories (required vs. merely supportive vs. irrelevant) to advance a conversation, rather than passively recalling facts, scored by compliance and integration metrics.
venue: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
task_format_metric: Strict Memory Compliance / Memory Integration Quality / Proactive Enrichment Score / Conditional Irrelevance Rate
example_length: 8.79 other:memory-items (average number of memory items in the memory pool per instance (overall)) | 9.81 words (average number of words per memory item)
what_instead_if_absent: the paper's own construct is 'strategic memory use' (defined precisely via must/nice/irr memory categories), not 'long-horizon' or 'long-term'; those terms appear only when citing prior memory-augmented-generation/long-term-dialogue benchmarks as related work
evidence_span: Under this trend, the ability to retain and utilize long-term memories becomes increasingly indispensable.

description_authors_words: We introduce KC-Bench, a controlled multi-turn benchmark for measuring this capability across world-knowledge conflicts, input inconsistencies, and multi-source temporal conflicts
description_summary: 238 multi-turn tool-use tasks (screened from 1,000+ candidates) testing whether an agent reconciles conflicting user instructions, parametric knowledge, and live environmental observations before acting, via stateful tools and deterministic environment assertions.
task_format_metric: human-verified/LLM-evaluator success score over multi-turn tool-use trajectories
example_length: 30 steps (maximum interaction steps per task before termination)
what_instead_if_absent: the term 'long-horizon' is used only to describe three of the nine evaluated backbone models ('recently released models designed for agentic or long-horizon tasks'), not to define KC-Bench's own task-length construct; the paper instead formalizes conflict types (world-knowledge, input-inconsistency, multi-source temporal) and caps interaction length operationally
evidence_span: we evaluate three recently released models designed for agentic or long-horizon tasks: DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.2, and MiniMax-M3.

description_authors_words: we study this as Evidence-State Revision, comparing flat retrieval, coarse edge invalidation, and fine-grained RevisionLedger on 2,907 high-agreement questions from GitHub, multi-repo issue histories, Wikipedia, and DyKnow-style temporal streams.
description_summary: 2,907 questions over self-revising records (GitHub issues, Wikipedia, temporal streams) test whether a structured memory mechanism correctly identifies which claims are current, superseded, or warrant abstention, controlling for a presentation confound that inflates apparent gains.
external_memory_evidence: RevisionLedger instantiates the fine- d d L 3 L_{3} architecture: a frozen LLM extracts atoms from a closed attribute inventory, a rule scorer labels co-keyed pairs, the ledger operator maintains current/deprecated sets and unresolved status, and the answer generator sees only the rendered ledger and an event-id index.
task_format_metric: QA accuracy under render-matched controls comparing flat retrieval, coarse edge invalidation, fine-grained ledger memory
what_instead_if_absent: the paper never uses 'long-horizon' or 'long-term' for its own construct (Evidence-State Revision); those terms appear only inside citation titles of related work (e.g. 'Memanto: ... for long-horizon agents', 'Mem0: ... scalable long-term memory') and are never applied or defined for ESR-Bench itself
evidence_span: Memanto: typed semantic memory with information-theoretic retrieval for long-horizon agents.

description_authors_words: we construct the Spatial Memory Benchmark (SMB) from EgoLife multi-day recordings, targeting capabilities absent in existing benchmarks: semantic trajectory retrieval and long-horizon object retrieval.
description_summary: From multi-day egocentric recordings, tests whether an embodied agent can retrieve when and where a specific object was in a given state, and track an object's motion trajectory, over hours-to-days-long observation.
external_memory_evidence: The Text view aggregates LTE motion captions, room labels, and parsed speech transcripts behind a vector index.
task_format_metric: success rate (frame retrieved within ground-truth temporal span, bounding-box IoU>=0.3) for Semantic Trajectory Retrieval and Long-Horizon Object Retrieval
example_length: 50 hours (length of an individual EgoLife recording session used to build SMB) | 2–24 hours (temporal lookback window per Long-Horizon Object Retrieval (LOR) query)
long_horizon_definition: [operational-threshold] a memory representation in which the state transitions of dynamic objects remain queryable in natural language across hours-to-days observation horizons
evidence_span: Embodied agents performing long-horizon tasks require a memory representation in which the state transitions of dynamic objects remain queryable in natural language across hours-to-days observation horizons.

description_authors_words: On a prespecified hash-frozen 3,600-case GPM-ReleaseBench, GPM matches all complete outcomes; the strongest of three intentionally simple complete policies matches 1,800/3,600 and makes unmatched releases on 50% of violation cases.
description_summary: 3,600 hash-frozen cases testing whether an agent correctly withholds or releases a claim depending on whether supporting memory records are contradicted, superseded, retracted, deleted, or stale, under a fail-closed release policy.
external_memory_evidence: We introduce Governed Persistent Memory (GPM), an auditable bitemporal state-transition model with source-bound admission, derived lifecycle state, current public barriers, and fail-closed structured release.
task_format_metric: exact match of complete outcomes on a hash-frozen case set; sealed end-to-end cluster correctness
what_instead_if_absent: 'long-horizon' appears only in the title ('... for Long-Horizon Agents'); the cached page is the arXiv abstract landing page, not the paper body, and the abstract text itself never uses or defines the term
evidence_span: Governed Persistent Memory: Source-Bound State Semantics and Fail-Closed Release for Long-Horizon Agents

description_authors_words: We introduce HUSH-Bench, a controlled benchmark of 2,400 benign prompts paired with histories containing one marked sensitive disclosure and matched no-memory references.
description_summary: Tests whether a conversational agent's long-term memory leaks a marked sensitive disclosure into an unrelated current-turn response without the user inviting it, scored by an unsolicited-history-integration rubric.
external_memory_evidence: We evaluate four models under no-memory, full-context, and three retrieval-based memory settings.
task_format_metric: Unsolicited History Integration Score (UIS, 0-100, condition-blind rubric) plus exact-target exposure rate
what_instead_if_absent: the paper uses 'long-horizon' only once, citing prior evaluations ('long-horizon question answering') as related work it distinguishes itself from; its own construction is described as starting from 'long-horizon, LoCoMo-derived personas' without ever stating a length/session threshold for what counts as long-horizon
evidence_span: Its construction starts from long-horizon, LoCoMo-derived personas, adds controlled history manipulations, generates benign probes, and filters examples, following established practice in personalization evaluation.

description_authors_words: We introduce SocialPersona, a benchmark for evaluating whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can recover revealed preferences from longitudinal social-media timelines and use them in dialogue.
description_summary: 171 real users' longitudinal social-media timelines (text+images, 2,597 verified preference tags) testing whether an MLLM can infer stable vs. recent interests from natural multimodal traces and personalize dialogue accordingly.
task_format_metric: interest-domain/tag F1 for profile construction; interest coverage/concreteness/fluency (LLM-judge) for personalized dialogue generation
example_length: 176.81 other:posts (average posts per user timeline) | 130.38 other:images (average images per user timeline) | 0–200 other:posts (maximum posts per user timeline (collection cap))
long_horizon_definition: [operational-threshold] a per-user timeline of chronologically ordered posts (text, visuals, timestamps) spanning at most 200 posts over a two-year window, from which stable interests (recurring across the timeline) must be distinguished from recent interests (concentrated in the most recent 90 days)
evidence_span: a temporally ordered timeline S_u = <p_1,...,p_n> ... spanning at most 200 posts over two years.

description_authors_words: We evaluate MEMORA with MEMORA-Bench, a 45-hour egocentric-video suite that measures both retrospective memory faithfulness and prospective memory-grounded planning.
description_summary: An embodied agent must recall past egocentric-video experience faithfully and use it to plan future actions, tested across 45 hours of video via separate retrospective-QA and prospective-planning scores.
external_memory_evidence: MEMORA organizes experience into participant-specific Environment, Entity, Activity, and Inferred Knowledge stores: online editing revises memory as new evidence arrives, while offline consolidation abstracts repeated experience into reusable routines, habits, and preferences.
task_format_metric: EAM-QA accuracy (retrospective memory faithfulness) plus Robot-Grounded Plan score (prospective memory-grounded planning)
example_length: 8–15 sessions (egocentric-video sessions per participant used to build each participant-specific memory bank)
what_instead_if_absent: the paper states that 'MEMORA addresses long-horizon context accumulated through a participant's ongoing experience' but never pins down a duration or session threshold for what counts as long-horizon; the 45-hour/8-15-sessions-per-participant construction is reported as dataset scale, not tied explicitly back to defining 'long-horizon'
evidence_span: MEMORA addresses long-horizon context accumulated through a participant's ongoing experience.

description_authors_words: We introduce ContextWeave, a longitudinal benchmark that evaluates whether recalled experience improves downstream agent performance in realistic office-work streams... reconstructs privacy-preserved, multi-month workflows of 14 participants into 1,005 executable tasks
description_summary: 1,005 executable office-work tasks reconstructed from real multi-month participant workflows test whether an agent's recalled experience actually improves downstream workspace quality and preference alignment, not just retrieval accuracy.
external_memory_evidence: Table 1 highlights the distinction between summary-oriented memory and in-context experience. Summary-based systems perform well on semantic relevance and precision but remain weaker in evidence coverage, solvability, and downstream performance. In contrast, a-mem , a representative of ICL-style memory, provides broader historical coverage, stronger continuity, and a larger reduction in exploration. The structured task-level summaries produced by langmem fall between these two regimes.
task_format_metric: Workspace Score and Preference Score (task-outcome quality), plus diagnostics of relevance, continuity, solvability, and robustness to misleading recall
example_length: 36300–212300 tokens (message-log tokens per task (average 36.3K, longest 212.3K)) | 20 other:subtasks (temporal-distance threshold (in subtasks) separating short-term continuity from long-term episodic dependency)
long_horizon_definition: [operational-threshold] the benchmark distinguishes short-term workflow continuity (a dependent task's relevant preceding task lies within an average of 20 subtasks) from long-term episodic dependency (a distance of more than 20 subtasks), with 24.4% of core tasks falling into the latter category
evidence_span: 75.6% of the tasks had an average distance of no more than 20 subtasks between their relevant preceding tasks, demonstrating significant locality; however, 24.4% still depended on earlier history with an average distance of more than 20 subtasks, indicating that the benchmark simultaneously includes short-term workflow continuity and long-term episodic dependency.

description_authors_words: We introduce UserToolBench , a benchmark for personalized decision making in tool-use LLMs.
description_summary: 10 user profiles across 36 tool sets and 1,065 multi-turn trajectories (170 tools) built from sanitized real interactions, testing whether a tool-use agent infers latent user preferences, asks for clarification, and acts consistently under incomplete information.
task_format_metric: personalized tool-call trajectory accuracy under incomplete information (lack-of-information, single-tool, multi-tool task types)
example_length: 106.5 turns (average turns per user profile (1,065 total turns / 10 profiles))
what_instead_if_absent: the paper repeatedly calls its trajectories 'long-horizon' (multi-turn trajectories, long-horizon reasoning, long-horizon behavioral consistency) but never states a turn/session threshold; it instead reports total scale (1,065 turns across 10 profiles) without connecting that number back to a stated definition of 'long-horizon'
evidence_span: The benchmark is built from privacy-sanitized real interaction traces and combines structured persona profiles, public API-style tool ecosystems, and long-horizon multi-turn trajectories.

description_authors_words: we introduce CL$^2$GEC, the first Continual Learning benchmark for Chinese Literature Grammatical Error Correction, designed to evaluate adaptive CGEC across multiple academic fields.
description_summary: Tests whether a grammar-correction model sequentially fine-tuned across 10 academic disciplines retains earlier-discipline accuracy instead of catastrophically forgetting it, using standard GEC and continual-learning transfer metrics.
venue: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
task_format_metric: GEC precision/recall/F0.5 plus continual-learning metrics (Average Performance, Backward Transfer)
example_length: 10 other:tasks (sequential disciplines (tasks) in the continual-learning curriculum)
what_instead_if_absent: the paper never uses 'long-horizon'; its one use of 'long-term' ('long-term retention is a critical objective') describes a baseline method's property in the discussion, not a definition of the benchmark's own scope. The benchmark instead formalizes its difficulty axis as a sequential stream of N discipline-specific tasks under the continual-learning (CL) paradigm, measured via catastrophic forgetting and Backward Transfer (BWT)
evidence_span: This supports the underlying design of GEM, which constrains gradient updates to protect earlier tasks-making it a strong candidate when long-term retention is a critical objective.
scope_flag: this is a continual-learning (catastrophic-forgetting) benchmark for Chinese grammatical error correction across academic disciplines, not an agentic long-horizon-execution or persistent-memory-store benchmark; its relevance to this charter rests solely on the 'forgetting' construct via sequential task adaptation, and it was tiered 'relevant' rather than 'core' by curation

description_authors_words: We introduce OceanGym, the first comprehensive benchmark for ocean underwater embodied agents, designed to advance AI in one of the most demanding real-world environments
description_summary: Eight underwater task domains where MLLM-driven agents must fuse optical and sonar perception with memory for long-horizon exploration under low visibility and currents, compared directly against human-expert performance.
external_memory_evidence: OceanGym agent maintains an explicit memory
task_format_metric: task success across eight underwater task domains, MLLM-driven agent vs human-expert comparison
what_instead_if_absent: the paper repeatedly says agents must 'achieve long-horizon objectives/goals' but never states a step-count, time, or episode-length threshold; the term functions as an unexamined descriptor of task difficulty throughout
evidence_span: Unlike static decision or generative models, these agents must integrate rich multimodal sensory streams and execute continuous-control policies to achieve long-horizon objectives.

description_authors_words: We introduce RealICU, a hindsight-annotated benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) under realistic ICU conditions, where labels are created after senior physicians review the full patient trajectory.
description_summary: 30-minute ICU data windows, hindsight-labeled by physicians reviewing the full patient trajectory, test whether an LLM assesses patient status and recommends actions correctly, rather than merely imitating possibly-suboptimal historical clinician behavior.
task_format_metric: hindsight-labeled task accuracy (Patient Status, Acute Problems, Recommended Actions, Red Flag) at each 30-minute window; Hit@5
example_length: 0–1800 hours (length of ICU-stay trajectories evaluated (ICU-Evo maintains performance for stays up to 1,800 hours)) | 30 other:minutes (length of each evaluation window (the benchmark's atomic unit)) | 930 other:windows (total windows in RealICU-Gold across 94 ICU stays (~10 windows per stay))
what_instead_if_absent: the paper's title/framing term is 'long-context' (long-context ICU data), and it mentions 'long-horizon reasoning' only once (describing what ICU-Evo's structured memory improves), without defining a threshold; its own formal evaluation unit is the 30-minute window sampled at a 2-hour stride
evidence_span: We further introduce ICU-Evo to study structured-memory agents that improves long-horizon reasoning but does not fully eliminate safety failures.

description_authors_words: we introduce SkillMisevo-Gym, a lifecycle-aware harness that versions skill state across agent frameworks, and SkillMisevo-Bench, a frozen design from malicious exposure to carryover tasks, with concept-aligned benign tasks and nine lifecycle metrics.
description_summary: Tests whether an unsafe action a self-improving coding agent took once gets distilled into a reusable 'skill' that later causes harm in unrelated benign tasks, tracked across nine lifecycle metrics.
external_memory_evidence: Each task runs in a fresh sandbox with a new conversation, workspace, process namespace, and tool session; only the episode-scoped skill store advances.
task_format_metric: carryover attack-success-rate (ASR) across authoring, retrieval, and fresh-session execution lifecycle stages; nine lifecycle metrics
example_length: 25 other:episodes (episodes per evaluated agent-method configuration (SkillMisevo-Bench)) | 525 other:tasks (tasks per evaluated configuration (225 malicious learning + 225 benign evaluation + 75 clean-session persistence tasks))
long_horizon_definition: [contrastive] 'long-horizon benchmarks' (as an existing category the paper distinguishes itself from) study accumulated memory across a session/task stream, whereas this paper's own object of study is agent-authored, persistent skill/procedure artifacts that are versioned and reused across separate task episodes -- a related but distinct form of cross-task persistence
evidence_span: Long-horizon benchmarks study accumulated memory rather than agent-authored skill files (Xie et al., 2026; Cheng et al., 2026). These designs therefore do not jointly attribute risk to the update, persistent artifact, retrieval, and later execution.

description_authors_words: We introduce DeepWeb-Bench, a deep research benchmark that is substantially harder than existing benchmarks for the current frontier... each task requires massive evidence collection, cross-source reconciliation, and long-horizon multi-step derivation.
description_summary: Deep-research web benchmark scoring agents across Retrieval, Derivation, Reasoning, and Calibration on tasks demanding massive cross-source evidence collection and long multi-step derivation, with source-provenance audit trails.
task_format_metric: per-cell rubric scoring across four capability families (Retrieval, Derivation, Reasoning, Calibration), with source-provenance audit
example_length: 8 other:entities (entities per DeepWeb-Bench task) | 8 other:dimensions (capability dimensions per task) | 64 other:cells (independently scored cells per task (8 entities x 8 dimensions))
length_unit_families: UNCLASSIFIED:other:cells; UNCLASSIFIED:other:dimensions; UNCLASSIFIED:other:entities; agent steps / actions
long_horizon_definition: [contrastive] long-horizon multi-step derivation is the requirement to compose retrieved evidence into a final quantitative answer through several layers of arithmetic and modeling assumptions across multiple steps, as opposed to a single extraction step
evidence_span: We target difficulty from three properties of the data itself: massive evidence collection rather than a handful of pages, cross-source reconciliation rather than single-source lookup, and long-horizon multi-step derivation rather than a single extraction step.

description_authors_words: we curate a real-world long-horizon benchmark of streaming app-usage trajectories, covering 12 scam types, spanning extended periods (15 days on average), involving diverse applications (95 apps), and interleaving normal and scam behaviors
description_summary: Tests whether an agent can anticipate an emerging smartphone scam from partial, streaming cross-app usage trajectories (15 days average, 95 apps, 12 scam types) before fraudulent intent becomes explicit.
task_format_metric: early-warning detection coverage, alert timeliness, and reliability over streaming app-usage trajectories
example_length: 15 days (average temporal span per long trajectory) | 96 other:app-events (average app events per long trajectory)
long_horizon_definition: [operational-threshold] a long-horizon benchmark of streaming app-usage trajectories spanning extended periods (15 days on average), involving diverse applications (95 apps grouped into 12 categories), with each long trajectory averaging 96 app events aggregated from many short traces
evidence_span: The dataset features extended temporal spans (15 days on average), diverse application interactions (95 apps grouped into 12 categories), and interleaved normal and scam behaviors. It consists of 57,662 short traces aggregated into 3,061 long trajectories, each averaging 96 app events and covering 12 scam types.

description_authors_words: We introduce LongWebBench, a benchmark for evaluating long-horizon webpage generation from both structural and functional perspectives... LongWebBench contains 490 real-world long webpages for structural fidelity evaluation and 507 goal-oriented interaction tasks over 129 webpages for functional evaluation.
description_summary: 490 long real-world webpages for structural-fidelity scoring and 507 goal-oriented interaction tasks over 129 pages for functional testing, evaluating whether a VLM's generated long webpage stays structurally coherent and remains actually clickable.
task_format_metric: multi-dimensional VLM-based structural-coherence metric (W-VFR); DOM-augmented agent-based functional verification (W-FFR)
example_length: 3–10 other:viewports (typical vertical viewports (screens) needed to display a W-VFR webpage) | 1–30 other:viewports (full observed range of viewport counts across the dataset, including the longest pages)
long_horizon_definition: [operational-threshold] the long-horizon nature of a webpage is measured by the number of vertical viewports (screens at fixed 1920x1080 resolution) required to display it end-to-end; most webpages span 3-10 viewports, about 31% exceed 10, and some extend up to 30
evidence_span: To characterize the long-horizon nature of W-VFR, we measure the number of vertical viewports required to cover each webpage under the fixed 1920x1080 resolution. As shown in Figure 3(a), webpages exhibit a long-tailed distribution. Most webpages span 3-10 viewports, while pages exceeding 10 viewports account for about 31% of the dataset, with some extending up to 30 viewports.
scope_flag: this benchmark measures the length/structural complexity of a GENERATED artifact (a long webpage, quantified in vertical viewports) and executable multi-step interaction on it, rather than a persistent memory store or an agent's own multi-session execution history; it is closer to a long-context generation-fidelity benchmark than a long-horizon-execution or long-term-memory benchmark, though W-FFR's goal-oriented multi-step interactions give it some agentic-execution character

description_authors_words: we introduce the first plan-level closed-loop benchmark dedicated to plan-level agentic reasoning in dynamic real-world environments.
description_summary: Tests whether an agent's global tool-use plan remains coherent and robust across a long closed-loop execution in a dynamic environment, rather than scoring only step-wise tool selection accuracy.
external_memory_evidence: For stateful executable evaluation, each prediction is replayed against real tools, policies, and databases under strict forward-only execution; the submitted split contains 140 trajectories and the expanded study uses up to 800.
task_format_metric: plan-level closed-loop success rate / Tool Exact-Match under strict forward-execution, built on a tau^2-bench-derived executable trajectory split
what_instead_if_absent: the paper repeatedly invokes 'long horizons'/'long-horizon tasks' to describe where step-wise tool-chaining accumulates error, but never states a step-count or trajectory-length threshold defining the term; its own formal construct is a plan-level closed-loop protocol built on tau^2-bench's retail decision phases, without connecting phase count back to a stated horizon length
evidence_span: existing methods predominantly rely on a step-wise paradigm that optimizes one discrete decision at a time, limiting their global planning perspective and causing errors to accumulate over long horizons.

description_authors_words: We introduce EvolveScaler, a code-driven framework that defines information evolution before rendering it as natural language... Executing validated simulators produces natural-language multi-turn event histories, while deterministic replay computes reference answers and atomic checklists
description_summary: Simulator-generated multi-turn event histories, where later events revise or revoke earlier facts, test whether a model can track valid state and answer correctly given approximately 7 to 1,200 accumulated events, verified by deterministic replay.
task_format_metric: avg@5 / pass@5 accuracy on deterministically-replayed state-reconstruction questions, stratified by five difficulty tiers
example_length: 7–1200 other:events (events per instance, spanning five difficulty tiers from shortest to very_long)
what_instead_if_absent: the term 'long-horizon' never appears anywhere in the paper; the paper's own named construct is 'information evolution (IE)', defined as a setting where later events revise or revoke earlier records so that valid state must be reconstructed from an ordered event history -- explicitly framed as a difficulty axis distinct from context length or turn count alone
evidence_span: Solving an IE task requires identifying valid records, applying updates in order, and reconstructing the query-relevant state from the event history.

description_authors_words: we introduce the Episodic Memory with Questions and Feedback task (EM-QnF).
description_summary: Interactive extension of egocentric episodic-memory video QA where, after an initial possibly-wrong answer, a simulated user gives clarifying feedback and the model must refine its localization of the queried moment across three video benchmarks (Ego4D, GoalStep, HD-EPIC).
external_memory_evidence: Episodic Memory with Natural Language Query (EM-NLQ) retrieves specific moments from a person’s past visual experiences, such as wearable-camera video, using free-form text questions
task_format_metric: R1@IoU localization accuracy on natural-language episodic-memory queries, with and without interactive user feedback
example_length: 529–1014 other:seconds (video duration in seconds across EM-NLQ datasets (Ego4D-NLQ ~529-548s; GoalStep-Q ~960-1014s)) | 10.75–31.6 other:seconds (response-span (answer segment) duration in seconds)
what_instead_if_absent: the paper never uses 'long-horizon' or 'long-term'; it repeatedly describes the setting as requiring search over a 'long egocentric video' without ever stating a duration threshold distinguishing 'long' from short video
evidence_span: In episodic memory with natural language queries (EM-NLQ), a user may ask a question (e.g., "Where did I place the mug?") that requires searching a long egocentric video, captured from the user's perspective, to find the moment that answers it.

description_authors_words: We construct the AES-Bench, which covers 112 real-world GitHub instances across 9 programming languages. Each instance is version-locked, contains executable tests, and reflects authentic build and dependency practices.
description_summary: Tests whether an agent can set up a working, version-locked build/dependency environment for 112 real GitHub repositories across 9 languages, verified by running each repo's own executable test suite rather than just checking exit codes.
external_memory_evidence: EnvPilot maintains an expandable Trajectory-Derived Memory (TDM), initialized with 667 high-quality experiences.
task_format_metric: Pass@1 success rate on repository environment-setup tasks
example_length: 50 other:iterations (maximum agent iterations allowed per AES-Bench environment-setup task episode)
what_instead_if_absent: the paper's own environment-setup task/benchmark is never framed as 'long-horizon'; the term appears only in related-work citations describing OTHER memory systems and their tasks (e.g. 'HiAgent: ... solving long-horizon agent tasks', 'techniques improve retrieval relevance in long-horizon reasoning tasks'), never applied to AES-Bench or EnvPilot's own task structure
evidence_span: Rather than serving solely as a cognitive aid for long-horizon reasoning, recent work increasingly treats memory as a structured repository of actionable experience, capturing concrete execution outcomes such as configuration decisions, failure patterns, and validated actions.

aliases: T I D E; Temporal Information Drift in Evolving Documents
description_authors_words: We present TIDE, an expert-verified benchmark of 3,050 QA pairs over 644 official customs instruments issued between 1969 and 2025 by the Government of Bangladesh, covering eight task types over deeply code-mixed documents
description_summary: Legal/customs documents whose amendments explicitly state what they replace and when, testing whether a model resolves which document version was in force on a queried date rather than treating an old fact as simply overwritten.
external_memory_evidence: index it in ChromaDB
task_format_metric: strict/partial accuracy via three-judge LLM council with a hard date gate
example_length: 9.9 other:clauses (authoritative clauses prepended as context per query (mean |C|)) | 360–50829 words (source-document length (median words per instrument, over which a query's context is drawn))
what_instead_if_absent: never uses the terms 'long-horizon' or 'long-term'; frames the challenge instead as 'version resolution' over 'evolving documents', which it does define precisely
evidence_span: Evolving documents, such as laws, tax codes, and software documentation, are amended, replaced, and sometimes reverted over time, so a question has different correct answers at different dates.

description_authors_words: We present CivBench, an open-source benchmark for evaluating language model agents in long-horizon, tool-mediated environments through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).
description_summary: 300+-turn episodes playing Civilization VI via 76 MCP tools test whether an agent proactively monitors latent strategic state and executes commitments it made in its own earlier planning reflections.
external_memory_evidence: All non-local state must be accessed through explicit queries, allowing us to distinguish between information that is unavailable and information that is available but not retrieved.
task_format_metric: tool-call trace analysis: Proactive Monitoring Rate, Reflection-Action Gap (RAG@10), win/loss
example_length: 300 turns (turns per episode (single game playthrough)) | 1000 actions (tool calls per episode (order-of-magnitude, 'thousands'))
long_horizon_definition: [operational-threshold] A single episode spans 300+ turns and produces thousands of tool calls over a large action space, requiring sustained planning, state monitoring, and execution under partial observability.
evidence_span: We present CivBench, an open-source benchmark for evaluating language model agents in long-horizon, tool-mediated environments through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). A single episode spans 300+ turns and produces thousands of tool calls over a large action space

description_authors_words: we present VoiceLongMemEval (VLME) benchmark, where every answer depends on paralinguistic metadata (emotion labels, prosody descriptors, and voice events) attached to conversational turns, which is otherwise unrecoverable from the words alone.
description_summary: Tests whether a voice assistant recalls not just what was said across a long multi-session conversation but how it was said (emotion, prosody, voice events), with questions answerable only from audio cues, not transcript text.
task_format_metric: accuracy (blind vs. descriptive-transcript conditions, 3-seed mean)
example_length: 4–12 turns (turns per LLM-authored evidence session) | 26–26 turns (evidence turns per instance (upper bound))
what_instead_if_absent: cites 'long-term conversational memory' as an established measurable capability from prior work (LoCoMo, LongMemEval, PerLTQA) without itself defining the term; the paper's own contribution is instead defined around the paralinguistic axis (affect/tone) layered onto that existing setting
evidence_span: While long-term conversational memory, and paralinguistic perception have both become measurable capabilities, the two axes

description_summary: Controlled multi-step testbed of 200 tool-agent workflows testing whether a tool-augmented agent's entity binding (e.g. which account or record a step refers to) silently drifts or compounds errors across sequential steps, including under an entity-lock fix.
task_format_metric: per-step wrong-entity rate, drift rate, compounding factor (wrong actions per affected workflow)
example_length: 3–8 steps (action steps per workflow (primary carry entity persists across this many steps))
what_instead_if_absent: a related-work section heading borrows the label 'Long-horizon agent memory and state management' to categorize prior work, but the paper's own object of study is defined as multi-step workflows (3-8 steps) with a persistent entity-binding state, never itself termed or thresholded as 'long-horizon'
evidence_span: Tool-augmented language-model agents execute multi-step workflows over external systems, resolving an entity once and then acting on it across subsequent steps.

description_authors_words: We instantiate E-P-R on WebArena and on MemTrapBench, a controlled benchmark we build to isolate these phases.
description_summary: Tests how an agent consumes conflicting retrieved memory during a multi-step web trajectory, isolating whether a wrong memory changes an action (entry), persists (propagation), and whether the agent recovers afterward.
external_memory_evidence: Existing work mostly treats memory as a supply problem, asking what experience to write, how to store it, and which entry to retrieve for the next task.
task_format_metric: Entry-Propagation-Recovery (E-P-R) diagnostic: action-divergence deltas, propagation factor, recovery rate
example_length: 15 steps (browser-task trajectory length (median steps per task))
long_horizon_definition: [operational-threshold] The paper's own MemTrapBench operationalizes 'long-horizon' browser tasks as a 231-task subset (plus a 16-task pilot) with a median trajectory length of 15 steps, distinguishing them from short single-step interactions.
evidence_span: 231 long-horizon (median 15 steps) browser tasks on a shared HTML/JS skeleton served through BrowserGym.

description_authors_words: we introduce the Unintended Long-Term State Poisoning Bench (ULSPB), a bilingual benchmark comprising 350 settings spanning five assistance categories, seven interaction patterns, 24-turn routine interactions, and matched single-injection counterparts.
description_summary: 350 bilingual settings of ordinary 24-turn routine conversations (plus matched single-injection counterparts) testing whether benign chat alone gradually and unintentionally poisons a personalized agent's persistent state toward riskier authorization and autonomy.
external_memory_evidence: risky edits concentrate in memory-centric artifacts rather than being uniformly distributed across state files. Across models and variants, MEMORY.md and memory/ contain the largest share of risky edits.
task_format_metric: Harm Score (HS): authorization drift + tool-use escalation + unchecked autonomy
example_length: 24 turns (turns per routine user-agent interaction/conversation)
long_horizon_definition: [explicit-stated] Long-term state is the persistent, cross-session state that personalized agents maintain (authorization boundaries, tool-use defaults, autonomy level) to support long-horizon collaboration; the paper formalizes 'unintended long-term state poisoning' as the risk that routine, benign user-agent interactions gradually and cumulatively reshape this persistent state, weakening confirmation boundaries and escalating autonomous behavior over time, distinct from standard usability failures because it is persistent and cross-session.
evidence_span: Unlike standard usability failures, the risk is persistent and cross-session; it manifests when ostensibly benign interactions are recorded into long-term state and later executed as implicit, unsafe behavioral defaults.

description_summary: 120 simulated healthcare agent trajectories under escalating workflow disruptions, examining whether an agent's recovery behavior and consideration for affected stakeholders hold up as technical and human challenges accumulate over repeated interactions.

example_length: 3 other:challenge-phases (sequential challenge phases per trajectory (light, medium, heavy), each retaining the preceding conversation and unresolved outcomes)

evidence_span: Building on this view, we define considerate participation as situated adaptation that accounts not only for whether the focal task advances, but also for affected people, the agent's role and authority, and the surrounding workflow.

description_authors_words: we present WorldBench: a comprehensive, multilingual benchmark of genuine, persona-grounded everyday workflows, where agents can act in a sandbox via structured actions
description_summary: Tests multilingual, culturally-grounded agents on 1,600 persona-grounded everyday workflow tasks across seven languages and eight cultures, scoring both task completion and whether the agent preserves environment state.
external_memory_evidence: WorldBench individually checks whether any non-target file differs between the initial and final sandbox states.
task_format_metric: Constrained Task Success (CTS): task completion + minimal modification/state preservation
example_length: 30 steps (iteration cap (maximum agent actions per task before forced termination)) | 20 other:distractor-artefacts (distractor artefacts included per testbed alongside target files)

description_authors_words: we introduce ParaGUIBench, to our knowledge, the first benchmark dedicated to parallel execution and coordination of multiple GUI agents on separate desktop instances... a dataset of 233 tasks spanning six task categories; and an evaluation system with efficiency metrics, including step reduction ratio and token cost.
description_summary: 233 GUI tasks across six categories run on a multi-device Docker infrastructure with a shared file system, testing whether multiple GUI agents coordinate sub-tasks in parallel across separate desktop instances, scored on success rate and efficiency gains over serial execution.
external_memory_evidence: The infrastructure runs concurrent workers that share a file system.
task_format_metric: task success rate + step reduction ratio + token cost (parallel vs. serial execution)
example_length: 75.9 steps (mean critical-path (perception-decision-action) steps per task under the strongest serial baseline (Claude Sonnet 4.6)) | 38.7 steps (mean critical-path steps per task achieved by ParaGUI's parallel planner-worker execution on the same tasks)
what_instead_if_absent: uses 'long-horizon tasks/workflows' as an unexamined descriptor of GUI agent difficulty throughout (contrasted qualitatively with costly per-step LMM inference and degrading context), without stating a step-count or duration threshold; the paper's precise formal definitions are of parallel length L_parallel, total length L_total, and parallelism degree P=L_total/L_parallel, not of 'long-horizon' itself
evidence_span: However, current agents scale poorly to long-horizon tasks: actions incur costly LMM inferences, and performance degrades as context grows.
